Commentary on the Vāruṇapaddhati by T. N. – 143.
Commentary on the *Vāruṇapaddhati* (The *Varuṇapaddhativṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śivottama). Om.
An Explanation of the Varuṇapaddhati Ritual Manual.
Hariḥ Oṃ.
By stating the seed-syllable (bīja), the source of its origin, or the purpose of its application, the true nature of both initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is correctly understood.
In this regard, first of all, the venerable Varuṇa—
having placed before him the object intended to be presented, which is the form of his chosen deity and the auspiciousness of all beings, and having paid homage to the Teacher— proceeds.

The practice of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), which has been performed through tradition, is made known even within one's own self as praise for a portion [of that conduct]. Through the authority of one's own words, an inclination toward that [conduct] arises in the listeners;
thus, the subject matter [is introduced] preceded by a salutation to the chosen deity.
He explains:
"Homage to Soma, the source of bliss, who possesses the two seeds of Nirvāṇa; now, the two seeds of initiation and installation are summarized. (1)
Having paid homage to Śambhu— who is accompanied by Umā and Soma,

and who is therefore the seed of the two types of liberation (nirvāṇa), being the cause of the two-fold supreme good— thereafter, through the relationship of door and gateway between initiation (dīkṣā) and installation (pratiṣṭhā), [he explains] the two types of liberation...

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: we have here summarized that which is the cause (*nidāna*) or the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the activity of the two things that constitute the means (*sādhana*). This is done for the sake of easy comprehension. Likewise, agency is not possible even for Śiva, who possesses external characteristics.

Therefore, it is well said that the state of being the seed of the two types of liberation arises through Umā, who is of the nature of the Supreme Power (parā-śakti) and serves as the instrument, and not by means of [the Self] alone.

Furthermore, that which is nirvāṇa— characterized by liberation from bonds such as impurities (*mala*) and the manifestation of the self’s own nature (*svarūpa*), and synonymous with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—
is of two kinds due to the twofold nature of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For instance, one limiting adjunct is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Kaivalya, which is called Nirvāṇa, occurs in initiation without a substratum (*niradhikaraṇadīkṣā*); thus, through these two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is a twofold division of Nirvāṇa.
In both cases, Śiva alone, accompanied by His Śakti, is the cause. Others, however, say that when...
In the isolation (*kaivalya*) of consciousness, first there is the characteristic of having *prakṛti* as its substrate;
this is the supreme *nirvāṇa*, also known by the synonym "attainment of *aṇimā*" and so forth.
However, it is distinct from that *kaivalya* which is the liberation from the continuous bondage of the diseases of pleasant karma.
[The claim that] for human beings, the scope [of practice] consists of bondage and liberation, and the manifestation of Śiva-nature through the direct realization of prior karma— this is incorrect.
For even if powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth were merely specific forms of worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*), the state of supreme beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*) would still exist [as a distinct goal].

Others, however, maintain that initiation (dīkṣā) alone is the single liberation; for otherwise, once initiated, liberation would only occur after the collapse of the body, due to the attainment of a dual nature— as in the case of an uninitiated youth,
or as in the case of one whose body remains as it was before.
Just as a second birth is accepted through the rite known as *upanayana* by the authority of the scriptures,

so too here [in this system], liberation (*nirvāṇa*) is attained through initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is called "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*). Yet even that does not constitute the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*), because it does not transcend the state of experiencing worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*).
Others, however, say that there are two types of nirvāṇa according to the sequence of the two types of birth (yoni).
Indeed, the birth of a person is twofold: that which consists of the mother’s womb and that which consists of the material cause of the universe.

And as it is heard [in scripture]: "The One presides over womb after womb. Therefore, there is one final birth known as Nirvāṇa; beyond that, because there is no further birth for the person (puruṣa), even the womb which is the material cause of the universe, having been exhausted, results in the manifestation of Śiva-nature.

The claim that "nirvāṇa is twofold due to the distinction between the higher and the lower" is also untenable; for it does not escape the aforementioned refutation, as it does not transcend [the state of] enjoyment (*bhukti*). Likewise, even liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) resulting from yoga is not the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), because it does not transcend enjoyment. Therefore:

The first explanation is indeed superior; for even though there are two types of initiation (*dīkṣā*) due to Śiva’s twofold manifestation, it is only *niḥśreyasa* (liberation) that constitutes the immediate fruit, and not [the fruits] resulting from initiation and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Thus, the presentation of the two is made according to the view that there are two kinds of *nirvāṇa*.
Why is it not performed? We say it is because there is no restriction regarding the two types of *nirvāṇa*.
For indeed, through various rites beginning with those for long life and ending with the yoga of Śiva, there are many paths to *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good) alone.
If initiation alone were the means [to liberation], then because it would lack a specific causal restriction, the two-fold nature of liberation could not be established.
It is therefore established that the two-fold nature of liberation exists only through the restriction of the two-fold nature of the means. Now, following the order of exposition:
Regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), its definition and its seed-syllable, he says:
"That action by which the state of Śiva is manifested through the dissolution of the three bonds is called initiation; it is characterized by devotion and dispassion. (2)

By that very action through which the two-fold result is produced, the superiority of the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*) over other ritual acts is expressed. It is thus stated that eligibility for initiation consists in the characteristics of devotion (*bhakti*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). This is the primary cause (*nidāna*).
And it has been stated that devotion toward Śiva and detachment from worldly existence are the two motivators;
having observed these two, characterized by grace, one must establish the respective domains for each.
Otherwise, because devotion and detachment would have fixed domains [without such distinction], they would conflict with one another.

This has been explained. It is stated that he who possesses devotion toward Śiva and detachment from worldly existence has no qualification for initiation (*dīkṣā*). This is because initiation is the fruit of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), and initiation is characterized by that [descent]. Therefore, it is the descent of power itself [that constitutes the qualification].

The seed of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the injunction [itself], because initiation is prompted by its fruit. Therefore, one should not initiate someone whose capacity has not been awakened by the instruction of the teacher and who has not fallen from their power. Now, how is it known that devotion and dispassion can arise even when there is a defect in the purification of the fire?

This is not a fault. Since the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) alone is the cause of that knowledge, one might ask: "What is this so-called 'descent of power,' given that power is all-pervasive? To this we reply: although it is all-pervasive, because the equipment for liberation is absent even when [the soul] is turned away [from grace], it is metaphorically designated as a "descent" (*pāta*) on account of its being accompanied by [the aforementioned conditions].
And its occasional nature is caused by the occasional occurrence of that "equality of karma" which acts as its co-operative cause. As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*:
"In the beginning, by the will of Śiva, there was the infinite Śaivī [power] which bestows the goal of Śaivism. She...
The primordial power descends upon a person in their final birth.
The impurity that causes saṃsāra belongs to one who does not fall away from that [state]; when that [impurity] is exhausted, there is direct attainment of supreme beatitude.
"Having approached a guide and received initiation, with his bonds severed, he—
purified and free from affliction— attains union with Śiva. Thus it is said.

In this context, karma has been presented as a cooperative cause, like a collaborator; as it is stated in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*, "it shines forth," and thus it is not elaborated upon here.
If the body is indeed the basis for spiritual practice, as it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"When equalized karma has arisen here through the power of time, one who has been initiated by a Guru through the descent of the intense power (*tīvra-śakti*) should perform worship."

Just as devotion and detachment are the signs of initiation, so too in Śiva’s world-cycle (saṃsāra) should its sign be understood; for it is known that through the union of devotion and detachment within Śiva’s world-cycle,
the descent of power (śaktipāta) alone is the cause of knowledge even for one whose impurities have not yet been exhausted.

With the intention that the expansion of the impurity of objective phenomena (*bhāva-mala*) occurs out of fear once the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) has been obstructed— since this is the cause for the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*)—
he concludes by summarizing what was stated previously:
"Therefore, knowledge, devotion, and dispassion [arise] from the Self."
These are the marks of one who has been initiated here; these belong to Yaśas, not directly to me.
Therefore, the soul whose power has fallen away is indeed a bound animal (paśu); for him, devotion, knowledge, and dispassion do not arise directly or with speed, even from a cause;
in this matter, it is the descent of power (śaktipāta) alone that is the prerequisite for initiation (dīkṣā). Otherwise, these qualities would belong to one who has already been initiated.

The signs do not exist; they do not come to be. For one who has been initiated, the signs are determined to be knowledge, devotion, and dispassion. This initiate is indeed one whose power has fallen away.
Therefore, for that purpose, they state here in sequence: first, the equilibrium of karma; then—
From that comes the descent of power (śaktipāta) upon Śiva; from that, knowledge; from that, devotion;
from that, detachment from worldly existence; from that, the search for a teacher; and from that, the attainment [of the teacher] for the sake of manifestation.
And from that [initiation] comes consecration (*dīkṣā*), from that the severance of bonds (*pāśavicchitti*), the manifestation of Śiva-nature,
and supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*). For that purpose, knowledge [is obtained] from Śiva, such as the venerable *Kāmika* and other [Tantras].
The defining characteristic of the Śiva-scriptures is that, divided into numerous primary and secondary branches, their universal sovereignty is attained.
As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Now, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of karma, known as the impurity of the self and Māyā, and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva..."
From Śiva, knowledge proceeds.

"Though that [consciousness] is one, it becomes manifold, arising from the lotus-like mouths of Śiva; through the distinction between the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā), it proceeds toward its objects by taking refuge in them. Thus [it is said].

But surely, for one who has been initiated, there is the study of the Śiva-scriptures; therefore, how can initiation be the cause of knowledge regarding Śiva? It is not the case that the purpose of initiation is characterized by the Śiva-scriptures alone; rather, it is for the sake of one whose power has fallen away.

Due to the power of that variety, there is no contradiction in the knowledge characterized by the acceptance of the existence of Śiva, which holds that "the Lord exists" merely as a worldly convention.

Now, since it has been stated that these [rites] do not apply directly to one who is without a sacrificial animal (*apaśu*), and in response to the inquiry as to what kind of animal [is required] or what its defining characteristics are, the author states the specific details regarding those characteristics and their utility, in order to make known that even the understanding of the nature of the animal and its fetters (*pāśa*) constitutes the seed of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
He is slightly ignorant, sullied, and divided; he is the agent and the enjoyer of his own actions;
he is embodied, all-pervading, eternal, a transmigrating being, possessed of a Lord, and the sovereign master. (4)
Thus is the indication of the subject; "one who knows only a little" is stated to be the definition.
(p. 7) Furthermore, that which is other than this [definition], being merely a qualification intended to provide an illustration of the definition—
such as "How can this person be ignorant of anything?"— applies to the Lord (pati), the bound souls (paśu), and the fetters (pāśa).

Since everything is included within these [categories], how can this definition—"the Paśu is one who knows only a little"—be merely that of the Lord (pati)? For he knows only a little because of his omniscience; nor does he possess the three bonds (pāśatraya), since there is nothing remaining for him after their cessation.
For one whose self is liberated, because that state is distinct from the prior state of being a bound soul (paśu), initiation— such as *pratiṣṭhā* and others—
serves as the cause for the further disjunction from bonds;
since [the soul] is included within Power (*śakti*), and Power is included within the Lord (*pati*), it is indeed the Possessor of Power who [is the agent].

How, then, is the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) established for oneself? Since the capacity for knowledge and agency are equal [in both], yet the Lord lacks omniscience, the state of being a bound soul is likewise asserted. It has been stated that one is "stained" (*malina*); this indicates the existence of impurity (*mala*). Furthermore, it is said: "The agent and enjoyer of his own actions, enriched by a body. Thus, he is the agent.

Since it is the substratum of knowledge, where could its agency reside? Thus it is said to be the "experiencer" (bhoktṛ), meaning it is the agent of experience alone. When the question arises as to whose experiencer it is, one would normally say "pleasure, pain, and delusion"; however, [the author] indicates them by means of their causes.

Regarding the phrase "of one's own actions" (*svakarmaṇām*): the meaning is that actions do not possess the quality of being experienced in their own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), but rather solely through the experience of their results, such as pleasure and pain. By the use of the word "own" (*sva-*), it is indicated that the distinction in experience and the distinction in its causes are established for each individual soul (*pratyātmakam*).

To the question "What is the basis (*āyatana*) of enjoyment?", it is said: "the body and wealth. *Ṛddhi*, *atiśaya*, and *svāmin* are synonyms. That self (*ātman*) is not merely the body; rather, distinct from that [body] and independent of it, there exists the form of karma—consisting of the actions initiated by the owner—that constitutes the body's ownership, such as [rebirth as] gods, humans, and so forth.
It has been stated that this is due to the diversity of bodies according to their state (*bhāva*). (p.

8) Since agency and so forth cannot otherwise be accounted for, the existence of impurity (*mala*) and the like is the logical mark (*liṅga*); thus, impurity is the direct meaning of the word *mala*. In the absence of that [impurity], the nature [of the self] is that of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).
This is established because it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"If there is no impurity in the person, what has been done by the power regarding enjoyments? The meaning is that [the person] is distinct.
What is thereby obtained? We say: the refutation of the non-duality of the self (*ātmādvaita*). Not so.
Just as there may be the occurrence of bondage and liberation for that which is essentially one, like the separation from a fetter, it is for this very reason said:

"He is the agent and the enjoyer of his own actions. This is because the diversity of bondage, liberation, and so forth arises from the differentiation of its own nature; and indeed, such diversity exists. Therefore...

If living beings are diverse, what is the basis for the doctrine of non-duality? If [the self] is all-pervading and eternal, why is it that the intellect, the senses, and the body cannot be the experiencer?
Because there would be no connection with another birth, there would be no recollection of that [previous state]; thus, [there is no] rebirth...

Indeed, the state of being an enjoyer belongs to that which links together the objects of enjoyment; otherwise, there would be a lack of common substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the enjoyment and its causes. For this very reason, it is said to be "that which is to be refined" (*saṃskārya*).

For refinement (*saṃskāra*), consisting of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by karma and other factors, is that by means of which [the self] relates to those fruits occurring in another location.

The state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) is established. Moreover, its status as an enjoyer is observed to correspond to the karma acquired in other births. For this very reason, its initiation (dīkṣā) is also [established]; and because of its eternity and omnipresence, the fruit of initiation occurs in another place and at another time.

Because of the occurrence of being an enjoyer. How can this [self], which is dependent on another birth, possess agency and enjoyership over its own enjoyment? It is said: "With God" (*seśvara*), meaning that this [self] is under the Lord; by His impulsion.
9) Regarding the agent in experience, it is said as follows:
"This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord..."
One shall go either to heaven or indeed to the state of a horse. Thus it is said.

The characteristics of the bound soul (*paśu*) and initiation (*dīkṣā*) belong to one who has entered [the path] from birth itself, because it is precisely the bondage of impurity (*mala*) and so forth that must be purified; for this very reason,
he states the characteristics of the three bondages (*pāśa*) in their proper sequence:
The fetters (pāśas) are also to be known as threefold: impurity (mala), Māyā, and Karma.
Impurity is the innate fetter; it is mentioned first for the purpose of explaining its purification.
Between Māyā and Karma, attachment (rāga) is common to both, yet that which arises from Māyā is distinct from that which arises from the body.

And the final teaching is that [the bondage] born of karma is emanated; for since the bond of illusion (*māyā-pāśa*) is internal, one must accept that the bond of karma (*karma-pāśa*) is external in relation to it. Furthermore, while the beginningless, established wheel continues its flow...

Among the impurities (*mala*), there also exists a mutual relationship of cause and effect. If this were not admitted, the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the innate impurity itself would be untenable. For it is precisely the diversity of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka-vaicitrya*)—which has *māyāmala* as its direct cause—that serves as the immediate cause for both liberation and worldly experience.

On all sides, for Maya, because it has transformed according to the ripening of karma, it serves as the cause for experience; for this very reason, when karma is completely exhausted, liberation occurs for the person from both *mala* and *māyā*,
because in the absence of the cause, the effect cannot exist, due to their state of being mutual causes.

While the *cakravat* (wheel-like), *calādi* (moving and so forth), and other [states] are occurring, the adventitious nature (*āgantuka-bhāva*) of those [factors] has been indicated in their proper sequence. Now— [p.
Following the order of the enumeration, he first states the definition of impurity (mala):
"Impurity is impurity, it is ignorance, and it is that which obstructs consciousness. (4)

"Malam" (impurity) is the designation of the object to be defined; "aśuddhiḥ" (impurity) is its definition; "ajñānam" (ignorance) is that which establishes it; and "caitanya-nirodhakam" (the obstructer of consciousness) means that very ignorance is the impurity, in the sense that it is the obstructer of consciousness.
Now he describes the characteristic of Māyā-pāśa:
"Māyā is that from which arises the withdrawal of the principles (tattvas), beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth;
such is the collection of principles starting from Kalā and ending with Earth."

Thus it is said that [the suffix] is elided because of its inclusion therein. Now, the definition of action (*karman*) is stated: "Action consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)," which is the completion of the sentence.
Therefore, as stated in the *Svāyambhuva*, the cognition of the teaching of Dharma arises solely from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).
It is known that the soul (puruṣa) is conjoined with impurity (mala), māyā, and so forth, which consist of latent impressions (vāsanā). By these fetters (pāśas), the bound soul (paśu) is joined;
according to the previously mentioned sequence, each of these three fetters contains within it the cause for a specific variety of fruits.

He concludes with my own state of being: "Due to the ignorance of the bound soul (paśu), there is the connection with Māyā for the sake of experiencing karmas; thus, when he is bound by this triple bond (pāśatraya), it indicates both the apparatus for enjoyment and that which is beyond it."
That [creation] is like an illusion and so forth by the will of the Lord; liberation does not exist otherwise than through this. || 7 ||
The sense is that there is no cause for his liberation apart from the will of the Lord;
for without the will of the Lord, his liberation is not possible.

Therefore, because [the Lord] is the cause, when the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) occurs, it is possible for the entirety of experience, such as pleasure and so forth, to arise simultaneously through initiation (*dīkṣā*) corresponding to *prasaṃkhyāna*. Since experience exists, there is the simultaneous binding by fetters (*pāśabandha*) and, consequently, liberation; he explains this relationship between cause and effect as follows:

Then, by virtue of his own karma, he experiences the entirety of enjoyments such as pleasure; he is a transmigrating being bound like an animal, whereas the liberated one is freed from the three bonds.
Alternatively, the meaning of this sūtra is simply this: one bound by the three fetters is a transmigrator (saṃsārī), while one freed from the three fetters is liberated (mukta).
Now, desiring to demonstrate the different types of initiation (dīkṣā), for that purpose—
He begins to explain the threefold nature and the distinction of their essential forms regarding this initiation (*dīkṣā*).
This [initiate] to be graced is threefold: the *sakala*, the *pralayākala*, and the *vijñānākala*. He now describes these essential forms:
He who is covered by the impurities of māyā and karma is called sakala; he who is veiled by the impurities and karma is the pralayākala.
The connection with the Malaikabandha is called the Vijñānakala.
This is well-reasoned; now he demonstrates the division of the initiation of integration along with its cause:
"The grace of Śiva is twofold: without support and with support. (11)
In that context, the "clear meaning" (spuṭārtha) is said to be the adjunct (upādhi):
Śiva, independent of a teacher, is twofold due to the descent of power (śaktinipāta). || 13 ||
He himself bestows grace upon the stages of dissolution of consciousness.
In those who possess pure consciousness (*vijñāna*), the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is most intense and supreme; compared to that— (p.

"The supreme [grace] is intense during the [final] dissolutions"—thus is the twofold nature of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) stated. He describes another distinction regarding the supportless and the supported [grace]:
"By means of the fourfold descent of power, [the Lord] assumes the form of the Teacher (*ācārya*). (14)
The Blessed One bestows grace upon all of them as well.
The teacher possesses authority over the entire initiation, whereas Śiva alone is the actual agent of initiation;
the intention is that no one other than Śiva possesses the capacity to effect the severance of the bonds (pāśa).
Furthermore, there is a fourfold division of the descent of power (śaktipāta) based on its being very weak, weaker, intense, or more intense.

The cause for the states of dull-wittedness (*manda*) and so forth belongs to both the disciple and the teacher; furthermore, there are four types of these states, beginning with dull-wittedness. For it is not the case that all [disciples] are fit for grace (*anugrāhya*); rather, they are perceived according to an equal descent of power (*sama-śaktipāta*), and indeed, only because of the existence of gradations [in that descent]. Therefore, even when the teacher possesses excellence...
Grace proceeds in accordance with the gradations [of capacity] inherent in the disciple.

Thus, it is observed that not all teachers possess equal power; rather, because they may exist in states such as intoxication and so forth, it should be inferred that the bestowing of grace occurs in conformity with the [disciple's] disposition.

Now, since initiation (dīkṣā) has its seed in grace (anugraha), it follows that the process of initiation proceeds from that; thus he says: "For those who have performed their duties, initiation arises through the grace of Śiva. (15)

Those whose impurities are fully ripened are said to have "performed the work" (*kṛtakarmāṇaḥ*). By implication, it is established that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is prohibited for those whose impurities are not yet ripened. Therefore, initiation occurs again only among those who have performed the work. Furthermore, initiation is of many kinds; even among them, there is the ripening of impurity.
In order to elaborate upon the specific nature of initiation (*dīkṣā*) due to its manifold variety, [the author] begins (p.
"The various *vidyās* to be accomplished have been declared; now this elaboration of them is being stated."
And that [is] the means of recognition along with its substratum:
visual, tactile, verbal, and likewise mental initiation. (16)
The initiation of the teacher, the initiation of yoga, the initiation of the hotṛ-priest, and so forth, are of many kinds.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it is intended that [the offering of] water for the feet, the principal impeller (*pradhānapreraka*), the awakener (*bodhaka*), and so forth are included. Now, according to the instruction, he states the distinct characteristics of the ritual initiations (*karmadīkṣā*):
"Having opened his eyes and meditated upon that reality (*tattva*), he gazes at the disciple. (17)
This initiation for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the noose shall be visual.

Thus, and so forth, [the term] is *nirupādhika* (unconditioned). The word *tattva* (reality/principle) applies elsewhere than to Śiva; here, however, for the sake of that specific meaning, it refers to Śiva. Therefore, it is stated that Śiva is the true reality, the seed of initiation (*dīkṣā-bīja*) directly perceived by the mind; this is self-evident.
Having placed Śiva, complete with all his limbs, in his right hand.
One should touch the disciple’s head and other parts; this shall be the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā).
And so forth. Here too, the phrase "having meditated upon that reality" (tatvaṃ dhyātvā) is understood as carrying over from the previous context.
Because the conduct for the sake of initiation is rooted in that [reality], one should contemplate Śiva, who is joined with all his limbs;
that is to say, as the proponent of Śiva, [one should contemplate] the root-mantra of Śiva together with the six limbs, beginning with the heart.
"Having placed it in the right hand"—the rest has a clear meaning.
Having concentrated the mind upon reality, his inner splendor was increased.
One should recite the Saṃhitā mantras; this is proclaimed as the Āgama initiation (āgdīkṣā).

Because of such various concentrations upon reality (*tattva*), that which is called the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*)—intensified by the splendor of one's own self—is ignited and made manifest within the locus of its power. (p. 14)

It has been stated that the characteristic of the vocal initiation (*vāgdīkṣā*) is that one who has not attained the state of *śiva* should not recite the *saṃhitā* mantras as an *ācārya*. It is also stated in the *Śrīlaiṅga*: "The root [mantra], the Brahma-mantras, the limb-mantras, the form-mantras, the seat-mantras, the *saṃhitā*, and the teaching of Śiva."

"Relying upon a mental procedure, it is called 'mental' (mānasī)," and so forth. Whatever is to be accomplished by external action, all that being performed mentally is the "mental procedure" (mānasa-vidhi); by means of that, the mental initiation (mānasa-dīkṣā) becomes accomplished. By the word "and" (ca), [it is implied] here as well.
Having drawn [the mind] back by concentrating the mind on the reality previously described, it is called "mental" because it relies upon a mental procedure. || 20 ||
The initiation into the scripture (śāstradīkṣā) is declared to be through the transmission of the scripture.

Thus it has been stated. Now, one might object: in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra* it is said, "The initiate (*samayin*) who is capable is a person authorized in the scripture. How then can the definition of scriptural initiation (*śāstradīkṣā*) be described as being optional?

This is not a fault, because only one who has been initiated through the *samaya-dīkṣā* and other such rites has the qualification to hear the scripture; for it is only for the *samayin* that the attainment of another initiation occurs upon the transmission of the scripture.
Through yoga, there shall be initiation into yoga; that [initiation] is established in the state of Śiva-hood.

This rule of injunction (*niyamavidhi*) establishes that this yoga-initiation (*yogadīkṣā*) is ordained not merely for the state of being Rudra nor even for the state of being Īśvara, but rather specifically for the state of Śiva alone; or else,
it means that once Śiva-hood has been attained through *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*, the yoga-initiation follows in this manner.

The meaning is that it pertains to the authority over what is to be performed (*kartavya*). Alternatively, this Yoga-initiation (*yoga-dīkṣā*) does not culminate in the bestowal of the status of Rudra; rather—

The meaning of the aphorism is that [the state] is attained solely for the sake of manifesting Śiva-nature. Now, the definition of the *hautrī* (the female officiant of the *hautra* ritual) as specified is stated:
the *hautrī* possesses a *kuṇḍa* (sacrificial pit), and her *kuṇḍa*, maṇḍala, and so forth are outside the door.

The initiation consisting of the *samaya* and so forth, when being performed, is called *hautrī*. Thus, having stated the various characteristics of initiation along with its substrata (*sādhikaraṇa*), he now begins to state its twofold nature according to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). "That very initiation which is under discussion is indeed said to be of two kinds."
This indicates the specific distinction that the *hautrī* [ritual procedure] under discussion follows immediately after the initiation (*dīkṣā*) along with its formal basis (*sādhikaraṇa*).

The word "indeed" (*kila*) is easy to understand on its own. To clarify how it was introduced according to this very interpretation, he raises the doubt—"How is it that she is said to be twofold?"—and says:
For, in brief, this very knowledge is here called initiation by those who know it. || 22 ||

It is not as previously described in detail regarding its visibility and so forth; rather, this initiation is briefly of two kinds: that with a physical substratum (*sādhikaraṇā*) and, according to teachers who know its divisions, the "initiation free from the Kali age" (*akalidīkṣā*). Regarding this twofold division, the qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) is stated as follows:

"One is known as Jñānavatī (the Possessor of Knowledge) and the other as Kriyāvatī (the Possessor of Action). He explains that: 'Māyāvatī is that which possesses the fire of purification; through the correct realization of reality, awakening arises. One who possesses awakening through the correct direct experience of that Śiva-reality is [established] therein."

When it is stated that [the distinction] is abandoned due to differences such as place and time, but not for the practitioner and the teacher, it follows by implication that this applies to everyone else. (p.
The non-occurrence of the other [initiation] does not mean that it has not occurred at all; for since the seedless initiation,

which pertains to children, the simple-minded, and so forth, has already been performed, even if one accepts the exclusion of the *samayin* and *putraka* [from that], they still possess the seed in both types of seeded initiation.
By way of exclusion (*vyāvṛttyā*), there would be only that which possesses a locus (*sādhikaraṇa*) and is being led [to realization]. It is not the case that what is intended is something new;

thus, the non-exclusion of that [locus] becomes established as having a seed (*sabījā*) through valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). Regarding the phrase "due to differences of place, time, and so forth" (*deśakālādibhedataḥ*): what is meant? It is not that every place is [attained] through the perfection of the teacher (*ācārya-sampad*).
It is stated in the treatise that [the time] is free from defects; rather, it is distinguished by place and time.

Thus, in the treatises of the venerable teachers and those born of the lineage of teachers, the autumn, spring, and so forth, are praised as the times for initiation (*dīkṣā*). The word "and so forth" (*ādi*)...

Established as possible according to the aforementioned place and time, even silence in another place or at another time is praiseworthy; for one who knows the reality of the Lord's nature and possesses the supreme power to reveal the true character of birth, he is capable of accomplishing the purpose of seekers through his very presence among men.

They accept this state of being. For the specific characteristics of the body and so forth do not serve any purpose in initiation (*dīkṣā*) from the perspective of its essential nature; rather, because [the body] is difficult to obtain, it would simply be an obstacle to initiation.
Just as a twofold division has been stated based on the states of "with seed" (*sabīja*) and "without seed" (*nirbīja*), so too is there the "with seed" [initiation].
He further states that initiation itself is twofold according to its internal distinctions:
"Action, consisting of merit and demerit, which is future and manifold. (31)
Where purification is performed intentionally, that alone is called the Śivadharmiṇī initiation.

The fruit [arises] from the distinction between oblations and gifts, due to the enumeration of dharma and adharma— which are universal and eternal— as well as the enjoyments based upon them, and due to the distinction among qualified recipients such as those desiring enjoyment (bubhukṣu) and those desiring liberation (mumukṣu).
There would be no excess of distinction.
Likewise, regarding actions such as purification (*śauca*) which are to be performed with varying degrees of gravity or lightness.

It is thus established that "this is to be performed by those following the Śiva-dharma," "this by the Teacher," "this by the disciples," "this by those belonging to the same lineage," and "this by those belonging to different lineages.
In this way, by again resorting to another qualification, within the very context at hand—

Regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*) that involves a formal office (*sādhikaraṇā*), he states its twofold nature: "Because of the eligibility for the mere obligatory [rites], it belongs to the initiate (*samayin*) and then to the spiritual son (*putraka*); initiation without office (*niradhikārā*) is occasional (*naimittā*) and does not involve an office."

Initiation (dīkṣā) is of two kinds, distinguished as "with office" (sādhikāra) and "without office" (niradhikāra). Among these, let it be understood that for the *samayin* and the *putraka*, it is indeed "without office. Therefore, because they have authority only over the obligatory rites (*nitya*), they lack authority over occasional rites (*naimittika*); thus, it is "seedless" (*nirbīja*).

This is the same regarding the *dīkṣā* (initiation) category. For both the *samayin* and the *putraka*, initiation begins with the *samaya* (vow); thus, it is an initiation "with seed" (*sabījā*). This is because, by its very nature, it depends on the capacity for the threefold [activity] (*triyā*), and since that [capacity] follows from it and is not fixed, it is optional.
Having proposed the alternatives that [the practice] has seeds when there is the capacity for mindfulness (*satisāmarthya*) and so forth, and is seedless (*nibīja*) in their absence,

[the author concludes] that because it would lack a specific qualification (*anadhikāra*), it remains merely an alternative. Alternatively, he states the subject matter (*viṣaya*) for the purpose of the qualification:

Because the practitioner and the teacher possess authority in all matters— whether daily rites, occasional rites, or rites performed for a specific purpose— that [power] belongs to them both as one endowed with authority.
This is the explanation of the verse.

Now, taking as the subject matter the initiation into the pledges (*samaya-dīkṣā*)—whether it be with seed (*sabīja*), without seed (*nirbīja*), with a specific qualification (*sādhikāra*), or without qualification (*niradhikāra*)—the author demonstrates the twofold nature of the "seed" (*bīja*) in general:
Wherein there is yoga in the state of Rudra, and yoga in the state of the Lord of Sacrifice (Yageśvara).
That initiation in which there is no cutting of the topknot is of two kinds, pertaining to the Samayin.

It is stated that there is a twofold nature to the *samayadīkṣā* due to the attainment of the state of Rudra and the attainment of the state of Īśvara; because of the absence of the cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*), it is common to both.
But how can there be no cutting of the topknot (*śikhā*)? For even in the mere initiation of the *samaya*, the cutting of the topknot is prescribed in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuva*:
"For the sake of performing the three substances, one should perform the fivefold oblation."
"Having cut off your crest-lock at the end of the oblation, then perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order.

This is true; however, although this is stated in the *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*, in the divine scriptures (*divyāgama*) the cutting of the crest-lock is established as being an integral part of the initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*), because the instructions are found scattered throughout them.

Even when the *samayadīkṣā* (initiation of the rule) is being discussed, it is stated that it is "spoken of" (*ucyate*); therefore, it is appropriate to rely on this very scripture and other authorities. The aphorism states: "Where there is no cutting of the top-knot (*śikhāccheda*).

Now, with reference to the *nirvāṇadīkṣā* (initiation of liberation), since there is a distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhibheda*), the object [of the initiation] is qualified by those conditions (*sopādhika*).
Showing the distinction, he says:
"Where there is the severing of the bonds and the crest-lock, that becomes Yoga in the state of Śiva. (34)
"That very [state] is called Nirvāṇa through the consecration by the son. Thus it is said.

Having kept in mind that there are two types—namely, the cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*) and the cutting of the bonds (*pāśaccheda*), which serve as the causes [for initiation]—he establishes the scope of that which is devoid of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). He states: "That very [initiation] is for the *putraka* by means of consecration. This is what is meant:

The initiation known as *nirvāṇadīkṣā*, which does not have consecration (*abhiṣeka*) as its fruit, must be performed by taking only the *putraka*—who lacks further office—as its object. Consequently, the definition of the *putraka* has also been stated [by implication] from this very passage.
He who, having made a commitment through the vow of non-study (*niradhitā*), has severed the bonds and the top-knot through the initiation of Nirvāṇa, is called a *putraka*; furthermore,
that which results from the fruitless initiation is the twofold nature of one initiated into Nirvāṇa.
He states the seed [of this knowledge]: "And because of the consecration with the mantra to be accomplished, she is proclaimed as being in the practitioner. (35)
Through the consecration of all vidyās, she becomes the domain of the Ācārya.
One who desires accomplishment (*siddhi*) should indeed practice the mantras; likewise, one who desires liberation (*mokṣa*).

Accomplishments (*siddhi*) are characterized by qualities such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth. Furthermore, there are many kinds of tasks to be accomplished, such as rites for pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and subjugation (*kṣaudra-karma*). Not all mantras are suitable for every type of accomplishment.

However, the established rule is that [this applies] only to someone for someone else. That mantra which is capable of bestowing the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* and so forth, becomes effective for a practitioner desiring those powers provided there is no contradiction with his own name, birth constellation (*janmanakṣatra*), and other such factors; and for him—

Since only one who has been initiated into the practice possesses the requisite authority (*adhikāra*), it is precisely through such authority that an initiation corresponding to that [practice] bears fruit. This means that within the domain of the *ācārya*, the *ācārya* must be made the presiding agent (*adhi-kartavya*). Consequently, by virtue of having authority over all vidyās—

The term *ācārya* (preceptor) is established by its meaning as one who is both initiated (*dīkṣita*) and consecrated (*abhiṣikta*). That very [initiation] is of many kinds— possessing a locus (*sādhikaraṇa*), consisting of the rite of initiation (*dīkṣākriyāvatī*), possessing knowledge (*jñānavatī*), with seed (*sabījā*), without seed (*nibījā*), with entitlement (*sādhikārā*), and without entitlement (*niradhikārā*)— and pertains to the *samayin* and the *putraka*.
It is established that a formal arrangement must be made for the practitioners and teachers.
Now, with a reasoning that encompasses the intended meaning of everything previously stated, he concludes the whole by means of a single analogy.
(20) [It is] the bestowal of the state of Śiva upon one who is endowed with the purificatory rite of Śiva (śivasaṃskāra). || 36 ||
"Whether by means of ritual action or by means of power, that initiation is considered complete in every respect. Thus [it is said].
Because the bestowal of the state of Śiva (*śivatva-samarpaṇa*), by virtue of being the ultimate objective, pervades all forms of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Now, setting aside the fruit of initiation, he briefly states its definition according to its essential nature and the distinction of its causes:
In initiation, the embodied soul is said to be released from the threefold bond of existence.
And that purification of the path of initiation (dīkṣādhva-saṃśuddhi) is considered to be that sixfold path.

The threefold impurity consists of Māyā, Karma, and the form of worldly existence (rūpādbhava-bandhana); liberation for the embodied soul from these is the fruit of initiation (dīkṣā). The purification of the paths (adhva-saṃśuddhi) is the essential nature of initiation; the sixfold path is the objective to be purified, and initiation is the means by which it is purified—this is stated for the sake of defining the rule.

"Liberation for the embodied soul comes through initiation alone, and not by any other means. Nor is it the case that knowledge, yoga, and ritual action are thus rendered useless; for they serve as prerequisites for initiation.
He now demonstrates the nature and the sixfold division of these paths:
The path of mantra, the path of word, the path of phoneme consisting of worlds, the path of principle, and the path of energy—these twenty-one paths constitute Śiva. (38)

Next is the enumeration of the paths by way of their withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). Then, "dissolution" (*laya*) is indeed the state of being the locus of withdrawal within the pure [path]; this is the literal meaning of the word "purity.
And that [purity] belongs to the effect through the cause—that is the cause's [purity]—such is the intention of the author of the Sūtras, as has been stated.

"The twenty-first is the state of Śiva. In that regard, because of the manifestation of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and the teaching on the absence of obstruction, it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:

The path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*) and the path of word (*padādhvan*)—this is the state of Śiva (*śivapada*). It should be understood as the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*). For it is taught in that very [text] as follows:
"This is declared to be the reality of Śiva, situated above all paths. Now, one might object:

How can the dissolution of the sixfold paths into the Śiva-tattva be possible? For the dissolution of an effect occurs in its cause, and not elsewhere. Nor is it correct to say that the Śiva-tattva is the cause of the paths (adhvan), because it consists of pure consciousness, whereas the paths possess the nature of fetters (pāśa).

Because of consciousness. Furthermore, the disappearance and appearance of the interruptions of sounds (*dhvani*) cannot be the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*); likewise, since it is impossible for power (*śakti*) to be the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), the dissolution of sounds must be stated to occur in the material cause itself, and not elsewhere.

Some say that because the Śiva-tattva is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), the dissolution of the paths (*adhvan*) occurs within the Śiva-tattva; they maintain that it is not by way of being the material cause (*upādāna-tayā*), but rather solely as the efficient cause. Others, however, declare that this is incorrect, for when it is said, "One enters the state of Śiva," [it implies more than mere efficiency].

The entry of the paths (adhvan) occurs within the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa). Now, when there is the dissolution and purification of the paths, one who is purified in that reality becomes initiated and attains the state of Śiva;
thus, the "twenty-one" refers to that which is intended as the means for attaining the state of Śiva.

That is incorrect. Since it is stated here that the initiated one enters Śiva, the statement "the path (adhvan) enters" is intended as a metaphorical expression (upacāra) for that desire [to enter]. Furthermore, it has been said that the paths, such as the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), exist only through the acquisition of the levels of attainment (saṃpad) and so forth, according to the sequence of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).

Since the term "entrance" (*niveśa*) is used as a part of a word, it implies the inclusion of the other parts of that word as well; thus, even for one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*), there is no attainment of the Self through the mere entrance into Śiva.

(22) It is meaningful that she now causes [him] to enter; thus, in this sense, the metaphorical usage "she enters" is possible because of the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of both Śiva and initiation (*dīkṣā*). Furthermore:

In initiation (*dīkṣā*), the ritual act known as "union" (*yojanā*) must be performed for the self of the initiate toward the abodes of Śiva; however, that [union] is logically impossible for one who is already liberated. If you argue that it is a metaphorical union (*upacāra-yojanā*) in that case, then for one who asserts such metaphorical application everywhere, what [logical conclusion] follows? Thus, how can one maintain [the doctrine] through delusion?
The explanation: when Śivatattva itself is the material cause (upādāna), there arises from it a transformation known as *bhoga* (experience), which is the *bindu*.

From that *bindu*, the path of *kalā* (*kalādhvan*) manifests in the sequence beginning with *śāntyatītā*; furthermore, from the manifested path of *kalā*, the path of *tattva* (*tattvādhvan*) manifests.
Then the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvā*), then the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvā*), then the path of words (*padādhvā*), and then the path of mantras (*mantrādhvā*);

thus, in reverse order from the sequence of emanation, is the sequence of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*). By means of the *baindavī* [method], the six paths are led right there, and therein occurs the dissolution of the *bindu* known as enjoyment (*bhoga*).
This [notion] that "the Śiva-tattva" is the culmination of Śiva is also untenable;

for this is a conventional usage within the Śaiva system regarding the stages (parvāṇi) of the Śiva-tattva, Bindu-tattva, and Sadāśiva-tattva, which consist of dissolution, maintenance, and authority, and are mutually related as cause and effect.

Thus, it is established that the abode of Śiva alone, which is the material cause of the universe and endowed with existence, must be the locus of dissolution for all those bound by fetters who possess the *puryaṣṭaka*.
For it is precisely in that [abode] that the *puryaṣṭaka* is joined to the body during initiation (*dīkṣā*). Indeed, therein—

The dissolution of the bonds—namely, impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and so forth, as well as karma—is called "liberation" (*vimukta*). This occurs when, immediately following initiation (*dīkṣā*) from one whose bonds have been released, there is the manifestation of the *śivatattva*.
According to the teachings of the Śiva-scriptures, this is non-dualism (*akulatā*).

And this very meaning has been illuminated in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra* and established in the commentary on the venerable *Mataṅga*; therefore, the path [of mantras] follows that [authority].

The explanation of purity and non-decrease will now be given. In this regard, there may arise the following doubt: "In this Śiva-pakṣa, even though the paths are independent, how is it that Śiva, the Lord, pervades them? Does He do so as a pervader by means of dependence [on the paths], or otherwise? This is the concern.
Having thus presented [the argument], he begins to explain the matter exactly as it was proposed:
"Mantras, words, and phonemes are indeed pervaded on all sides."
This is a self-explanatory statement. Now, so that ease may arise through the purification of the paths (*adhvan*), he teaches the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in a favorable manner, saying:
"In this world, those principles (*tattva*) are pervaded by the *kalās* according to the sequence of the *kalās*. (40)
Having clearly contemplated [the impurity], that which is censured throughout the fivefold path must be purified. || 41 ||
The five kalās of the five paths are characterized by supreme pervasion; therefore, those very [kalās] must be purified after having been contemplated through initiation.

It is thus stated that by the purification of that [Self] alone, the purification of those five censured paths is accomplished. Now, indicating— as if with a mere hint— that the *kalās* are to be purified according to the order of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*), their names are given in sequence as follows:
It makes known that which has reached the intermediate state of Yama: "Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Nāgasī. (41)

From the heart, throat, palate, and eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should contemplate the single earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) in sequence within the Nivṛtti-kalā, which is characterized by endurance and non-endurance. || 42 ||
"The city of Kālāgni and the others consists of one hundred and eight [worlds]," and so forth. (43)
Sound is a single quality, but Sadāśiva is always its cause. (57a)

Thus ends the fifteenth [chapter]. In this way, the pervasion of the *kalās* containing the five paths (*pañcādhvan*) according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) has been stated as a constituent part of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Here, by means of the sequence of withdrawal as the basis, the reasoning regarding the bondage of the fetters (*pāśabandha*) begins from the external [level].
To the extent that the internal bondages are loosened, the ease of meditative cultivation is achieved;
for this is observed from various examples. For instance, when a tree or the like is being cut with an axe or similar tool, first the outer parts such as the bark are severed.
But afterwards, from that [wood], the wood and so forth whose essence has disappeared [are taken]. Thus, here too, it is proper to act in this way.
For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Those to be purified who are more internal, as well as those who are more external—when the external has been removed..."
There may be an internal sequence of actions.
"Thus, the sequence of time and so forth has been explained according to the order of their binding; and in the world, this determination of objects is seen to be based upon real entities."

Furthermore, when that which is contrary [to reality] has been removed, even for one who is constantly engaged in the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*), this very [process] becomes a cause for bondage because it relies upon the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*). [Objection: But how can even the phonemes (*varṇa*) of the words of mantra [be such a cause]?
The justification for the term "six paths" (ṣaḍadhvan) is as follows: Since both the Lord (pati) and the individual soul (paśu) are admitted to be all-pervading, motion is impossible;

and because motion is impossible, the purpose of going [to another state] cannot exist. Furthermore, if such movement were possible, there would be no distinction between the bound (baddha) and the liberated (mukta).
The path of the "ittham" (thus) cannot be a connection of the paths beginning with yoga;

it is not due to metaphorical usage (*bhūpacāra*), for that [connection] is impossible because the rite called initiation (*dīkṣā*), which consists of the purification of the bondage of fetters (*pāśabandha*), is sequential in nature.
And since this [universe] rests upon the transformation of the bonds such as *māyā* and the rest, that transformation also possesses the nature of those [bonds];
and because it proceeds through a sequence beginning with the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth, it is similar to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Thus, this has also been stated.
In the venerable Svāyambhuva [Tantra] it is said:
"Even though both the Lord and the individual soul possess omnipresence, the path for you two is as follows in the Drāviḍa [tradition]."
It is said: "Listen to that, O Brahmin, concerning the path of the person; for I have explained the rite of initiation in its proper sequence, since I am not yet fully perfected."
Since that path is a transformation, [it consists of] place and so forth, as well as lying down and so forth.

That very [process] occurs through the transformation of *māyā*, through the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and through the traversal of the paths (*adhvan*). Nor is this "traversal" merely figurative on account of similarity; thus, there is no contradiction here between omnipresence and movement, nor between liberation and movement. Or rather, this is the meaning of the word "movement": the fire of initiation...

"Because it is the seed of saṃsāra for the person (puruṣa), its state as liberation is [the realization of] its own true nature. This too has been stated in that very same work: "That which is the final state of the person, who is the seed of bondage and saṃsāra..."
Its movement is to be understood as such; it is not a state of remaining in another location. Thus [it is said].

Now, an objection may be raised: "In the statement regarding the pervasion of the time-periods (*adhvan*), since sound and the other elements are already included by the two compounds, a redundancy is observed. This fault does not apply, because [the elements] are included within that very same group of twenty-four principles (*tattva*) due to their pervading nature as the substratum (*pratiṣṭhā*). Specifically, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are subsumed therein.

In that regard, there is a distinction between the basis for the application [of the terms] *tattva* (reality) and *guṇa* (quality). Indeed, the basis for the application of the word *tattva* is its essential nature (*prakṛtibhāva*). Here, in the context of the interplay of actions, the word *guṇa* refers to the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) as that which instigates [action]. Thus, what is the cause [of this usage]? It is due to the difference in the grounds for their application.

It must be stated that the distinction [of objects] is established because the object itself is differentiated by way of the relationship between cause and effect; therefore, they are merely the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

The cause [is defined] as that which possesses qualities such as "first" and so forth, while the effects are the elements (bhūtas) along with their specific attributes; how then can there be identity of meaning? Thus, when this definition has been set forth, O wise one, there is some tautology regarding the pervasion (vyāpti) of the constituent parts.
He states the utility of the pervasion by time for the practice of initiation:
"Having thus reflected upon the paths, [one should contemplate] the Supreme Goddess who pervades the six paths. (57)
Having meditated upon that, one should then visualize the supreme state above it.

The meaning of the aphorism is as follows: one should contemplate that supreme state of Śiva—which consists of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), which pervades the aforementioned path (adhvan) employed for initiation (dīkṣā), and which is synonymous with dissolution (laya).
Having thus stated the utility of the six paths for initiation, [the author] now speaks of the internal [path].
Having reflected upon that which belongs to him, he begins to speak with reference to it.
Now, [he describes] the extent of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), which are employed in the initiation (dīkṣā), in their proper sequence.
The enumeration is here stated according to its divisions; for it is enumerated in accordance with the sequence of its own nature, following the order of its retention.
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, as well as Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna; [these correspond to] the heart and the head. (45)
The crest-syllable (śikhā), the dharma-mantra, and the root-mantra are declared to be the path of mantra (mantrādhvan). || 60a ||
This is the intended meaning.
Although there are millions of mantras,
and although mantras are infinite, all of them are encompassed by these eleven mantras alone, from *sadyojāta* up to the *mūla-mantra*, because they constitute their seed-syllables (*bīja*).
The reality of initiation (dīkṣā) is the state of the path of mantra (mantrādhva); this is taught in reverse order for these eleven [categories] mentioned [previously].
In this manner, [the application of] words (*pada*), phonemes (*varṇa*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth should also be applied.

Since these are innumerable, the pervasive word (*vyāpakapada*) and the rest constitute the path (*adhvan*) by virtue of being limbs of initiation (*dīkṣā*); therefore, through their purification alone, all mantras, words, and phonemes [are purified].

Because the purification of the worlds and other elements is thus established, this being the case, the eleven words associated with the *vyomavyāpin* mantra must be accepted in reverse order, exactly according to the path previously described. This is clear.
Thus, the path of words (padādhvan) is proclaimed to consist of exactly eighty-one words.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is declared to consist of the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'. || 62a ||
This is easily understood. Now, the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is described.
Or the Kālāgnirudra, the Kūṣmāṇḍa, the Hāṭaka, and the Brahmavaiṣṇava [Purāṇas]. (62b)
And so forth. From "In the kalā called Nivṛtti, one hundred and eight [worlds] are to be known" up to this point, the explanation is self-evident. Now, the worlds of the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā are described.
Amareśa—
"O Dadhi in Puṣkara," and so forth; these are explained by the *nigama* (Vedic citations).

Now, beginning from the reverse pervasion (*viloma-vyāpti*) of the Śrīkaṇṭhas, such as Mareśa and the others, up to the level of the *prakṛti-tattva*, [the text describes] the division of their respective substrata and the progression through the seven and eight groups (*aṣṭakas*).
And regarding the vision [of the deity], he summarizes the pervasion of the *pratiṣṭhā* and *kalā* [kalās]:
"Amareśa and others reside in the state of authority (*āptatva*), while Hariścandra and others reside in the state of splendor (*tejas*). (1.84b)
Gayā and so forth belong to the element of air, while Vastrāpada and so forth belong to the ether. || 85 ||
In the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) beginning with Chagalaṇḍa, the mind is situated in the [worlds] beginning with Paiśāca; thus, there are fifty-six cities, starting from Prakṛta and Avakṛta. 86a.
In the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), they are to be known by the names Amareśa and so forth. || 86b ||
Now, concerning the pervasion of the *vidyākalā*, he describes the worlds:
"Vāma, Bhīma, and likewise Ugra, Bhaveśa, and Anekacīraka," and so forth. (87a)
In the Vidyā of Vāmā and the others, there are twenty-seven Purāṇas. || 91a ||
Now, regarding the pervasion of the Śāntikalā, it is said concerning the world: "In the [kalā] that has passed, there are the five and ten worlds beginning with Nivṛtti. (97a)
Here, by means of the path already described, he concludes the great total number of all the worlds:
"In this way, there are two hundred worlds existing within the five kalās. (97b)
That which has been described as "the worlds" consists of twenty-four [plus one]. || 98a ||

The worlds are not merely those many [already mentioned], but there certainly exist others as well, distinct from these and taught in the divine scriptures. Nevertheless, for the sake of making initiation easy, we have set forth before you only this many which have been established by us.
The intended meaning is that although [these categories] are mentioned as distinct in the Śiva-āgamas, their inclusion within those [fivefold groups] is to be inferred.
Now, it may be asked: "The five *kalās* have been stated to be all-pervasive; what then of the *mantra-padas* and *varṇas*?"

Furthermore, in the *Śrīmatsvāyaṃbhuva* and other [Tantras], there is a rule that the pervasion of the paths of the other [categories] is manifested through the path of the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth. Consequently, this constitutes the actual reality of the meaning of the scripture; thus, because a real entity cannot withstand conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), this is not a fault.

Regarding the optionality of initiation (*dīkṣā-vaikalpya*)... [initiation] dissolves even those who have resorted to the paths (*adhvan*) of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth, which are the limbs of initiation in the divine scriptures (*divyāgama*).

If it is argued that even so, there is a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and so forth regarding the entity (*vastu*), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the entity consists of unity and its progressive increase, [we reply: this is true. That real pervasion is indeed one; it is of the nature of the *śaktitattva* (the principle of power), because the *śaktitattva* and *śivatattva* (the principles of Power and Śiva) face toward all the paths (*adhvan*).

Furthermore, since that [nature] exists in all six [categories], its actual attainment of duality—even though it is distinct—prevents its subsistence as a real entity. Or rather, because such pervasion is eternally constant (*kūṭastha*) throughout the three times, there is no cessation; however, one must determine what the reality here truly is. Moreover, this applies even to words (*dhvani*).

If one accepts the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), then because the path of *kalās* alone constitutes the pervasion, even in initiations involving all the paths (*sarvādhva-dīkṣā*), the non-establishment of the stages (*parva*) of the other paths must be accepted; thus, there is no connection with the five [entities] beginning with Sadāśiva as distinct from the *kalās*, which are the substrata of their presiding deities.
Even when [the mantra] is being uttered by means of word-delimitations (*padāvaccheda*), the array of words (*padavyūha*) is divided fivefold precisely by the five *kalās*,
because it is the *kalās* alone that directly effect the delimitation, as was stated in the context of the words pervading the path (*adhvavyāpipada*).

By virtue of being the essence of the syllable Oṃ, Śiva becomes the one who transcends peace (śāntyatīta), the supreme beyond the supreme; for the sake of the first limitation and again for the sake of the second limitation, among those established in the station of the all-pervading void (vyomavyāpin),
there is the path known as the five mantras.
The arrangement beginning with protection and ending with the forms of space and so forth is established within the seven-syllable word;
thus, for the purpose of the third limitation, it is characterized by five words beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *śiva*.
Therefore, one should know that the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is established at the beginning of the path of knowledge (vidyādhvan).
"From that [Ātman], one should know the principle of Vidyā (Vidyātattva), which is established at the beginning of the path of Vidyā. Thus,
the path [of Vidyā] is determined by taking the fourth limitation as its starting point and the fifth limitation as its limit.
"The path is established upon the foundation; the station of the thirty-two words belongs to the foundation.
That which follows Nivṛtti is proclaimed as the [other]...
And all of this has been explained by these [verses], and it is to be known from the venerable Svāyaṃbhuvatantra.

It should be viewed in this way. Therefore, even Varuṇaguru teaches that the pervasion of the path occurs through the *kalās* alone; thus it is established that "the path is here as we have described. Regarding the state of being the beginning and end within the world (*bhuvana*), he says:
Now, the thirty-six principles [are]: earth, water, fire, air, and space; || 98b ||
This and so forth is explained by the recitation of the text.

Now, regarding the path of the Kalās (kalādhvan), [the extent is as follows]: Śānti, along with another, namely Śāntyatītā—these are the five Kalās, beginning with Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti. Thus he concludes the section on the seed-syllables (bīja) concerning initiation (dīkṣā).

"The summary of the six paths" means that we have thus provided the summary of the six paths for those who understand the seed-syllables of Śiva-initiation; this is the intended meaning of the conclusion. Thus ends [the section] in the *Varuṇapaddhativṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śivottama.
The first chapter.
Now, desiring to demonstrate the seed of action as it was previously promised, he first states the primary seed:
"The entrustment of the power of action to the subtle body (liṅga), which consists of the power of knowledge."

The application of the ritual procedure for the *pīṭha* (seat), namely its consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), is stated to be summarized; this is the completion of the sentence. By this, the power (*śakti*) of Śiva is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the body, which is an infinite synonym [for it].
Having taken that very [reality] into one's heart, it becomes manifest as form through its locus;

and it is threefold by way of the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Among these, the *liṅga* consists of the power of knowledge, and the *pīṭha* consists of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)... [as performed] by the Śiva-teacher who knows the Self.

It is stated that the meaning of the term *pratiṣṭhā* is the act of conjunction (*saṃyojana*) performed according to the path taught in the Śiva-śāstras, by way of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, through the process of integration (*saṃgraha*).
Thus says Śiva himself directly, because of his being a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), by means of his supreme inherent nature (*samaveta*): [text fragment]...by his supreme [nature].

By means of the power of knowledge characterized as consciousness itself, it knows everything else by its own nature. It is precisely through that [power] that this [consciousness] is understood—both from scripture and through reasoning—to be the agent and the causal factor of the phenomenal world; therefore, only that much has been stated. Now...
"The presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Lord consists of His own power as its cause.

Since that power consists of both the instruments (*karaṇa*) and the presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Śiva, who is the Self, therefore this very power of ignorance (*ajñāna-śakti*) is His form (*mūrti*).

It is proclaimed in the scriptures. In common worldly usage, the referent of the word "form" (*mūrti*) is that which characterizes the self; however, since such a referent of the word "form" cannot literally be of the nature of the Self, and because it is impossible for the Self to be characterized by it, [the term refers to] that which is inherent in it.

Since it is the power whose essence is knowledge that first becomes perceptible, this is the basis for the metaphorical designation of "form" (*mūrti*); and because the *liṅga* is established as the form of Śiva,
it is brought about as being essentially the power of knowledge.
Because Śiva is the prototype [of all agency], his agency consists in being the substratum of knowledge;

thus it is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) alone that establishes his agency, while in that state, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is figuratively attributed to him. This is because, in the world, [agency] is pregnant with action.
Since agency belongs to that which is independent as the agent of action, there must also be a desire that expresses such independence; for [agency] is characterized by one's own will (*svecchā*).
Furthermore, because the independent Śiva possesses all desires simultaneously, he has no connection with a primary volition;
thus, it is his power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) alone that is metaphorically designated as "Śiva’s will" (*śivecchā*) by means of the aforementioned limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
Therefore, like the power of knowledge, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is also inherent to him.

Furthermore, the establishment of its status as "external" (bahiraṅga) is that it remains in that state for an eon (kalpa). And this very quality of being external is the reason why [the power of action] serves as the foundation (pīṭha) for the [power of knowledge];
with this in mind, it has been said:
"In the *liṅga* whose nature consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), there is the offering of the powers of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Thus it is said.

The explanation of that very seat (*pīṭha*) is "yoga according to the rule" (*vidhinā yoga*); the meaning of the word "rule" (*vidhi*) is practice in accordance with the scriptures. Therefore, this is also established here: that this entire universe is created as the locus of the three powers.

Because the meaning of the word "commencement" (ārambha) pervades that [word "creation"], and because that [meaning of creation] pervades the meaning of "commencement," it has been stated with this intended meaning: "Victorious is the Sun, who, by manifesting his three eternal powers, holds the parasol over the three worlds."
It originates from the object. The terms "Prabhu" and "Īśvara" indicate that this aforementioned *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) has various forms and is fivefold.
These fivefold *pratiṣṭhās* are: *sthāpana*, *sthitasthāpana*, and *utthāpana*.
Likewise, the ritual of installation (sthāpana) has also been fully described.
He states the definition of the arrangement of the five objects in their respective order:
"In the linga, preceded by the installation of the Brahma-stone, it should be joined to the piṇḍaka. (3a)
(3b) Bāṇa and others [established] separately on a pedestal when it was decayed or manifest, according to the sequence.
In that case where the rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā) is performed with the placement of the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) as the primary focus upon the liṅga...

In the case of [liṅgas] such as the *vyatka*, that which is being performed is designated simply by the term "installation" (*pratiṣṭhā*). However, where one first joins the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) and then joins the liṅga— whether it be made of *bāṇa*-stone and so forth, or of metal or gemstone— the [ritual] performed upon that *bāṇa* and other such materials [is likewise called installation].

The term *pratiṣṭhā* refers to the act of installation (*sthāpana*) for those established in ritual practice. *Utthāpana* is the restoration of what has decayed; its meaning according to the Sūtra is that after first establishing a pedestal, the placement of the aforementioned *liṅga* upon it is called *āsthāpana*.

Having first demonstrated the fivefold nature of the rite called *pratiṣṭhā* by means of its name and characteristics, he next states an alternative characteristic for the rite called *pratihava*, in accordance with other treatises:

The installation of the image and the presiding deity, accompanied by the principles (tattvas) and their respective lords, is performed there in eight or five ways; such is the ritual procedure for installation in some cases.

The eight forms (*mūrtayaḥ*) are the five elements beginning with earth, the sun, the moon, and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Among these, the Lord of Forms (*mūrtīśa*) is as follows: furthermore, Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, and Hara reside in the five elements, while Paśupati resides in the sacrificer and Candramas resides in the moon.

Some say that the eight presiding deities of the forms (*mūrtīśas*) are Mahādeva, Sūrya, Tvashṭṛ, Īśāna, and so forth; others [include] Varuṇa and Guru as the form and the presiding deity of the form, etc. He will state another sequence by means of this [text].
That shall be explained in that very place. This being the case, such is the meaning of the sūtra: where...

In the rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā-karma*), the placement of the image and the Lord of the Image (*mūrti-mūrteśa-vinyāsa*) is performed in eight ways; or, omitting the placement of the image and the Lord of the Image, [the rite proceeds] according to the sūtra to be described hereafter (p.
The *tūrya* [state] rests in five ways upon the indicated principles (*tattvas*) and the lords of those principles (*tattveśvaras*).
In both cases, the very act being performed is designated as the *pratiṣṭhā* rite; it is nothing other than that. Now, concerning the extraction of the *lakṣmī* [syllable]:
Reflecting upon that, he begins to speak:

"When the portion of Rudra is divided threefold according to the line of Brahmā, the meaning is that the mark characterized by the *lakṣma* (stigma) is in the two lower portions. The rest is easily understood.

However, one should maintain only this: whose mark is it? For there are many statements regarding this in the scriptures; indeed, in the Matsya Purāṇa, in the chapter on the gift of Purāṇas, the excellence of the origin of the Liṅga has been described.
Where there exists the light situated within the *liṅga*, that is the Lord Maheśvara;

according to that [principle], it is called the *vidyā-kalā-liṅga*. Because the jar resides within that light (*tejas*), and because Māyā is superior to that [light] due to its all-pervasiveness, the entire universe resides in that very [Māyā].

Regarding the statement "the derivation of the word *liṅga* is said to be from the leading (*nayana*) of the substrate of illusion (*māyopādāna*)," others say that the word *liṅga* is explained here in this scripture as "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*), because it is stated in the venerable *Liṅgapurāṇa*: [text follows].
The root of the linga is indeed without marks, yet it is called the unmanifest linga; that linga is said to be Śiva, and thus it is established as the Śaiva linga.

And the root scripture for this is as follows—in the Śivaliṅgasūkta: "The unmanifest Sthāṇu became Maheśa, Śiva, the eternal, the existent, the supreme sky," and so forth. Others, moreover, rely upon this very same scripture.
"This *liṅga* is indeed the supreme void (*paramavyomikā*), the very *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*)" (p.
And thus it has been stated by the authors of the Purāṇas:
"Space is said to be the *liṅga*, and the earth is its pedestal.
Others, however, say that all this which has been stated refers to the support of the gross *liṅga*,
because it is stated in the venerable *Dharmaśāstra*:
Within the central liṅga stands the supreme liṅga, measuring a span;
perfected through meditative absorption and hymns of praise, it is seen as being of the nature of Śiva. It is neither made of gold, nor silver, nor copper, nor crystal, nor pearl.

"Abiding as the mere object of focus, peaceful, absolute, and consisting of Śiva"—thus, that very definition, being extracted, should be considered its defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). Regarding this, some say that this is a defining characteristic of Paramaśiva; so it has been stated.

Because it exists as the *liṅga* of the supreme Śiva, it should be worshipped upon the *śivaliṅga*. If it is argued that its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) must be extracted because it is the supreme *liṅga*, then let the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) itself be its characteristic. That too is auspicious from head to foot.
