Since both the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*) forms (*liṅga*) are alike in being representations of Śiva’s form and are essentially identical in their nature as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), that which is indeed accepted here as the formal embodiment (*mūrti*) is,
in that regard, omniscient and consists solely of power; it is therefore distinct from [the other two].

Regarding the necessity of establishing the "mark of clothing" (*vastrapariliṅga*) here, some say as follows: since this world arises from and dissolves into the six paths of *māyā*, that which consists of the supreme sound (*paranāda*), the supreme point (*parabindu*), and its synonym, the supreme, is the "supreme mark" (*paraliṅga*) situated within the [central] mark. In that regard—
Others, however, urge: "In that case, the word *bhavat* [meaning 'you'] is imperishable (*akṣara*) because it is a cause.
It is stated in the illustrious *Svāyambhuva*: "Therefore, since the supreme proficiency arises from hearing [the teachings], how could there be a path for that which is beyond the head?
It must exist by means of the entire path, even while transcending it;
for if it did not exist, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) would not be possible as a defining characteristic. In this regard, the *bindu* is introduced.

The proponents of this view say: "There is no cause for the universe, which is an effect, other than Bindu, Śakti, and Śiva; therefore, Śiva is solely the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and not the material cause (*upādāna*), because he is of the nature of pure consciousness and thus lacks the state of being a primordial matter (*prakṛti*); furthermore, Śakti is the material cause."
Since the agency of Śiva and others has been excluded by the [previous] refutation of the Yāmala [view],
it follows by elimination that Śiva is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of the universe as an effect; thus,
by virtue of being the efficient cause, he is as if included within the category of causes through the process of elimination from the *Yāmala*.
Even though it has been established that [the Bindu] possesses the status of being the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*),

it must nevertheless be accepted that the remaining Bindu alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe, its defining characteristic, and its primary nature. Consequently, there is no non-existence apart from its manifestation.

Regarding the phrase "as is possible": furthermore, those who do not tolerate the eternality of even that [sound], yet accept what was previously stated by virtue of its pervasion (*vyāpti*), say for that very reason: "First of all, Śiva’s power alone is the cause of everything..."
The word *nañjanaḥ* [is used] as a negation. However, the entity called *laya* (dissolution) is what is termed the *śivatattva*, but it is not Śiva himself.
For if that which consists of dissolution were accepted as the substrate (*upādāna*), it would follow that [the substrate] is material; yet the world does not have Śiva as its material cause.

Since the Siddhāntin accepts certain transformations, the *liṅga* known as *laya* (dissolution) is here designated as the "intermediate *liṅga*" (*madhye pariliṅgam*). And this [designation] is intended as an illustration.

Now, those who truly know reality declare that this is the extraction of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Next, he demonstrates the detailed lines and so forth of the characteristic as it is being extracted.
In the measurement of the *liṅga*, the width of the mark (*lakṣma*) is one part;
the earth is depressed, and its line is nine parts in width.

By the word *liṅga*, the portion belonging to Rudra is meant; its *liṅgāyāma* is its length, and [the question arises] how many parts (*aṃśa*) of that [length] it occupies. Therefore, it is stated as "parts of a Jina" (*jināṃśaiḥ*), which means it is established [as such].
The measurement of the auspicious sign (*maṅgala*) on the pure ground is the width of the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) together with its lines.
The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: one should accept that which has the measure of the expansion of the *lakṣma* as its own dimension;
then, having divided it again into nine parts, the *lakṣmarekhā* (the boundary line) should be drawn so that it is equal in width and depth by means of one part. Now, the alternative view (*pakṣa*).
He demonstrates the measurement of the thread: "The path of the mark consists of two wing-lines; that field is divided into eight parts.
By rotating through six and seven parts, it is displaced; their union results from subtraction. (7)

The meaning of the sūtra is that, beginning from the long thread, two lines for the eyelashes should be drawn by means of rotating the thread. When the area [formed] by the rotation of the thread is divided into eight parts, one should exclude two parts and [retain] either six or eight parts.

In that field, according to the correct measurement, one should first rotate [the cord] like the moon according to the meaning of the sūtra, until the intersection of those two lines occurs at the installation of the *liṅga*; this has been stated.
Having thus shown the general protection for all *liṅgas*, now—
He shows that rotation in another manner (p.
"But when that field is divided by fire... * * *
For the sake of the prosperity of the continuity of the earth, by virtue of the exclusion of the lower half. || 7 ||
Regarding that field which was previously mentioned, when it has been divided into three parts, this is the specific detail:
having set aside the upper portion, one should arrange the remaining two and a half parts for the drawing of five lines. For what purpose?
For the sake of the prosperity of the lineage, when the five lines are drawn in a circular motion,
it is said that there should be a circle for the continuity of the eyelashes; thus,
while being extracted, the characteristic mark of the eye is intended for the purpose of the circular motion of the eyelash-lines.
"It shall be for the sake of the progenitor’s lineage and prosperity"—this is incorrect.
Immediately following the laying out of the thread (*sūtrapāta*), what is that laying out? It will be shown as being like that field (*kṣetra*).
Having established this as common [to all], when there is a distinction in its function, it is other than that.
Two methods have been described above as pertaining to the wearing of all the *liṅgas*.

However, in the case of specific rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*) or attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), that very same procedure must be performed differently. For example, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is accomplished by means of the ritual manual (*vidhāyaka*); that [manual] need not be shown here.

This is because we must state that it is merely the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which is established. Alternatively, from two and a half parts, there may be two sections (*adhikāra*), with one section being additional.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Having made [the measure] like the multiplier of half the *lamba*, of the two parts..."
"That sūtra is shared by those who desire both enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (mokṣa).

Therefore, this sūtra is appropriately established as being common [to both], because there is no exclusion of the common category regarding enjoyment and liberation; for there is a distinction in their respective functions.

Having thus stated [the definition] and having demonstrated the extraction of the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*) regarding the unmanifested (*avyakta*) and other signs (*liṅga*) because they are the objects of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and so forth (p. 39), now, first—
He establishes the defining characteristic for the face, the *liṅga*, and so forth:
"The opening of the eyes is the characteristic for the manifest (*vyakta*), and it is the characteristic for both the manifest and the unmanifest (*vyaktāvyakta*) [9b].
The 'manifest' refers to images and the like; the 'manifest-unmanifest,' however, refers to the face-linga (*mukhaliṅga*); the rest is easily understood."
Next, he describes the impairment of *lakṣya* (the target) due to differences in the object:
"It does not [occur] there in a moving object such as an arrow, nor in iron, nor even in one made of gemstone. (10a)
"The extraction of the characteristic mark (lakṣaṇoddhāraṇa) must be performed"—this is the completion of the sentence. On the pedestal (pīṭha), he shows the distinct characteristic:
in the middle of the opening, the pedestal-mark (lakṣmapīṭhaka) is shaped like a vulva (bhaga) with its tip pointing upward. 10b.
This is a sound method; however, for the purpose of drawing the root-line, one should draw that line from the root [of the hole] at a distance of one-third of the hole's diameter. || 11a ||
Like the *liṅga*, there are three parts; having first established the upper portion, one should rotate the hand from below across two parts so that the base of the vulva-shape is properly formed.

It is stated that [the cavity] should be made hidden by the *bhaga*-line within a space possessing an extent and depth corresponding to the lines of the characteristics of the *liṅga*. Therefore, it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Having carved out its characteristic, one should make a hole in the shape of a *bhaga*. Just so...
The supreme secret, consisting of power, is perceived by the worlds.

Thus, having extracted the characteristics of the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), one should perform the bathing of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya-mūrti*)— beginning with the pouring of honey, clarified butter, and so forth— with water from pitchers, decoctions, perfumes, milk, honey, and pure water. Then follows worship, the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), and the chariot procession (*rathayātrā*).
Having performed the placement of the jar for sleeping and so forth according to the ritual application as stated in the *Paddhati* (p.
the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu-sādhaka*) should proceed as will be described hereafter.

He states what must be performed after the placement of the *mūrti*, *śādi*, and so forth, upon the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the stone, in accordance with the specific qualification and desire [of the practitioner]:
"The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *liṅga*, the pedestal, and the stone is to be performed in sequence, starting from the *tattva*s. (11b)

The ellipsis of the sentence is that one should contemplate Śiva, Śakti, and Sadeśānta. In that regard, the pervasion of the pedestal by the Liṅga and of the stone by the pedestal should first be meditated upon in that sequence; thereafter, beginning from the Tattvas and so forth according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama).
One should contemplate the pervasion of the stones of the Liṅga-pīṭha by Śiva and Śakti respectively, as the nature of Power (Śaktitattva) and the nature of Sadāśiva. Beyond that,
within those very three [stones], one [should contemplate] the single function...

In order to effect the conceptualization of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*) through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and to bring about the realization of pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "One should again conceive of the three sections: [the first] ending with the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) and Śiva;
[the second] is Māyā; [and the third] is the region of Power (*śakti*). (12ab)
Sound, mind, and that which has spatial limits [are located] respectively in the liṅga, the pīṭha, and the stone.

This is what is meant: one should contemplate the *liṅga* as having three sections within its womb (*garbha*), by way of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader—consisting of *śuddhavidyā* at the bottom, *śakti* in the middle, and *śiva* at the top; likewise, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) consists of *māyā* at the bottom and [the rest] in the middle.

One should likewise conceive the pervasion of the three sections as being, respectively, of the nature of Śiva, of the nature of Śakti, and of the nature of the Tattva; thus, upon the stone slab, one should conceive the earth and the other elements up to the subtle element of sound at the bottom, the organs of action up to the intellect in the middle, and [the remaining principles] at the end.

One should conceive of the pervasion of the three sections as being composed of the principles of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) and so forth, culminating in Sadāśiva; this is mentioned here by way of incidental context.
He demonstrates the pervasion of the path through the jar of the heart (*hṛtkumbha*) by virtue of its being the locus of *prasāda*, as well as the conceptualization of it as having three sections:
"The pervasion of the reality-limit (*tattvāntika*) by me has been proclaimed for the jar of the heart. (13b)
Furthermore, the path of three sections consists of the mind, the digit [of time], and that which is enveloped by māyā.

This is well-connected through the preliminary ritual placement (*praṇyāsa*). Within this heart-pitcher, which has become the manifest form (*mūrti*), the six jewels and other elements should be placed; furthermore, within it, [the deity] should be conceptualized.
Then, when the heart-pitcher has become the manifest form, one should invoke the temple (*prāsāda*) by means of that embodied form.
The person named [Nāma] makes known the pervasion of the path by means of the three sections;
the threefold nature of the person extends as far as the person who is the limit of verbal cognition. 14b.

This is well-connected through the prior ritual placement (*prāṅnyāsa*). The state of the heart-pitcher being the embodiment (*mūrti*) is obtained through the reasoning that the dissolution-time [deity] has the conscious self (*cidātman*) as its form, and through the [scriptural] authority regarding the goat as its embodiment.
For it is stated in the *Piṅgalamata*:
Having invoked the Self-principle (ātmatattva), one should cause it to enter the path of the jar—
the pervasive Lord of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) who abides within the functioning of the self of all beings.
That [Self], whose nature is the favoring of karma, is endowed with the impurity of office (adhikāra-mala), accompanied by Niyati and the rest, as well as Kalā, Māyā, Rāga, and Vidyā.
Having meditated thus upon [the deity] as being attached to Māyā and Prasūti, one should then cause [the mind] to cease.
This is also logical:

since even a temple is a specific form of Śiva, just like the *liṅga*, and because the qualification for [the worship of] the forms of Śiva is prescribed without distinction for those possessed of impurity (*mala*), the state of being a manifest form of Śiva belongs directly to every image.
It has been stated incidentally that this is established in the commentaries on the *Śrīmataṅga*, the *Svāyaṃbhuva*, and other scriptures.
Now, in the context of the heart-vase (*hṛtkuṃbha*), by way of the conclusion, he demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which serves as the seed for the consecration of the doors and so forth:
"The pervasion of the doors, the temple, and the pinnacle is declared to be like that of the *liṅga*. (15a)
Having set aside the discussion on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*) as a digression, he teaches immediately after [the section on] pervasion (*vyāpti*):
"There, one should deposit the three principles (*tattva*) in sequence upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Antaka. (15b)
It is endowed with its own respective principles as lords, consisting of the self, knowledge, and Śiva.
Who [is it] that plants the three— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśāna— in the *liṅga*, indicated here in the singular by way of reference to them? Therein,
in accordance with what is indicated among those [deities], [it consists of] the *ātmatattva*, the *vidyātattva*, and the *śivatattva*.

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: one should meditate upon the three principles (tattvas) as having become manifest forms, endowed with the aspects of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, presiding over their respective principles; then, according to the stated method, one should install the lords (adhipas) into the mantra capable of being employed—which pervades those principles—up until the end of the *sparśahoma* offering.
This reality, which consists of the knowledge of the Self as Reality, is of the nature of Śiva;

this triad is essentially the state of the three powers (śakti). This is the established conclusion: the Śaiva reality, composed of power, pervades all effects and is superior, for it does not cease [to exist].

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, who are composed of all [principles], act as lords over the fettered souls (paśus) who are enveloped by the cycle of transmigrations, performing the tasks of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; yet, when their own authority comes to an end, they once again experience the ripening of their own karma here without obstruction.

Therefore, the liberated ones would not be superior with respect to the three powers (*śakti-traya*), and for each cycle of transformation (*parivṛtti*), Brahmā would be subject to complete transformation. In that case, how could the lordship over the triad of principles (*tritatva*) be established? This is not a fault, because [lordship] exists even among Sadāśiva and the others.
Because the meaning already stated exists: they too, being of the nature of offspring of Śiva’s form, are liberated at the conclusion of their own office. Even when these have been liberated...

It is said that within the cycle of transmigration, which is not subject to total cessation, the command of Īśvara proceeds as far as Sadāśiva. Even in that case, this same objection regarding excellence and deficiency applies equally.
If it is argued that even if such a state exists, the logical inconsistency remains as before, we say: no.

The persistence of that [state] is due precisely to the nature of the foundation of the Lord’s command; for indeed, enjoyment and liberation have been established by the Lord’s command itself—how could such a thing be consistent with a fault? Moreover, this is well known in the world. For instance:

Although the king alone is the direct sovereign over cities, villages, districts, and so forth, nevertheless, at that time, they are governed by his ministers; furthermore, for a certain period in the wilderness, they are again [governed] by the final [ministers]—this has indeed been witnessed by us. It is the same with Śiva.
The three powers, being supreme, bring all that [to pass]; since Brahmā and the others exercise their sovereignty over it only for a limited time, there is nothing inconsistent in this.
Now, in order to make known the specific arrangement of the placement of the forms and the lords of the forms, he says:
Where there are eight or five images, or when they themselves [are present]. 16b
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara themselves are the lords of the three principles within the Liṅga.
The eight forms— Earth, Fire, Sacrificer, Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Space— should be installed in each section.
Śarva, Paśupati, Agni, Rudra, Bhava, Īśāna,
Mahādeva, and Bhīma— these are the guardians of the eight forms.

The term "liṅga" is an elliptical designation; for in reality, the triad consisting of the pedestal (piṇḍikā), the craftsmanship (śilpa), and the presiding deity (tadadhipa) is intended, since their installation will be described later. For this very reason, it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:

In the parts of the *liṅga*, through the pervasion of the three principles (*tattva*), the purification of the paths (*adhva-śuddhi*) by fire-oblation, and the contact with Rudra and Īśvara as prescribed, there is no interval; likewise, having purified the ritual of the seat (*pīṭha-kriyā*) through pervasion, it is endowed with the Form (*mūrti*). That is the rite called "Action" (*kriyā*); such is the procedure here, but [it concerns] the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*).

The supreme Lord, whose nature is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), is all-pervasive and exists as the imagined subject of experience. Likewise, in that very place, Brahmā resides upon the stone slab as the common support for both the good and the bad;
he is the singular embodiment of the *sattva* among the principles (*tattva*s), and one should properly oppose him [in the rite]. This occurs in the third pure [state].
Or rather, the former [is] the activity of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.

How is it that knowledge and will are established one by one for each fragment [of the mantra]? In this regard, there is this distinction: the eight forms such as Yakṣman and the guardians of the forms such as Śarva are to be worshipped in sequence, even though they are essentially one; this has been well stated in other [scriptures] without exception.

The installation of the eight [deities] with the cane-staff and other implements, along with the thread, is performed by two [persons]. The placement of the forms (mūrtis) and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas) is eightfold or fivefold. Therein, the eightfold arrangement has been explained; the fivefold is experienced as the cessation of the pentad.

The arrangement of the five *kalās* from Brahmā and the other Lords of Causes, as well as the arrangement of the five Brahmans beginning with Sadāśiva, will be explained following the [relevant] aphorism.
Just as the eight forms (*mūrtis*) have been specified, so too, in due order, are the presiding deities of those forms.
It should be understood that they have been explained.

Thus has it been stated for the seeker of liberation; now, he describes another [form of] pacification of the form for the seeker of enjoyment on the pure path, beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Śakti. (19b)
In the consecration of the practitioner, Ananta and the others are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
In the pure Self, the attainment of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth would be the ultimate discourse.

The meaning of the words is as follows: according to the established doctrine of the divine scriptures (*divyāgama*), when the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is being performed for the sake of a practitioner (*sādhaka*) who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), the deities beginning with Ananta should be installed as the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipāḥ*) in each section; "outside" refers to this. Who are they?
In the phrase "Ananta and the others," he indicates them by name:
Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, and Ekanetra. (20b)
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkhaṇḍa, and Śikhaṇḍin; || 21a ||

The Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) have been described previously as being of two kinds; now others are seen [to be mentioned]. From Puruṣa up to Māyā, they belong to the pure realm, that which is of the nature of purity. (21b)
The Rudras, such as Aṅguṣṭhamātraka and others, are to be known by their sound and form. 22a.
The sense is that these indeed became the *mūrtipās* (guardians of the image) during the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of one desiring enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*).
Regarding the statement "of Ketu, [the guardians] are those measuring a thumb's breadth and so forth," he indicates them in sequence by their names.
And among the lords of the worlds who are the size of a thumb, Piṅgala is the sole one. || 22b ||
Udbhava, Bhava, and Vāmadeva of great splendor. || 23a ||
Thus, having shown the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), who are the causes of accomplishment on the impure path, he now demonstrates the established conclusion regarding the pure path:
"On the impure path, [the authority] over the observances (vratas) and so forth is established by them. (23b)
The guardians of the forms of the hundred Rudras are eight, stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Among the hundred Rudras, excluding those who are the lords of the directions (digīśas) both below and above, those who are the principal among the lords of the directions are the commanders of the hosts (vyūhapatayas).
Their intention is "May we dwell [there]. To the question, "By what names are they known? he says:
Asitāmbhoru, Uru, Caṇu, Krodha, Unmatta, and Bhairava. (25)
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas. || 27a ||
Those very same image-keepers who are defiled by that sin become the images themselves.
First, the fact that the earth, water, fire, and air [are the first four] is already established for the purpose of the eightfold division.
Having stated the variations regarding the forms (*mūrti*) in the case of the eightfold division, he speaks concerning the fivefold division:
"In the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of the five forms, [there are] earth, water, fire, and air... (27b).
The five forms beginning with Brahmā are the preservers of the five forms within the *liṅga* as stationary images.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "of one who desires enjoyment and of one who desires liberation. An option is stated for the seeker of enjoyment and the seeker of liberation:
"Or, for the seeker of liberation, [the deities] beginning with Nivṛtti are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) in the Foundation (pratiṣṭhā). (28b)
The five Lords, beginning with Sadyojāta, are considered to reside in the liṅga. || 28a ||

This is easily understood. Just as these powers have been stated in sequence for the *liṅga* during the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*), so too should they be applied to the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and Śiva respectively.
In this manner, the same procedure should be performed for the pedestal and the stone; this is what is to be declared. (32b)
The meaning is that this [subject] will be explained by the commentator as it is about to be stated; the distinction is that he himself will state it. He states its designation:
"Action, knowledge, and likewise will—these are considered the presiding deities of the three principles. (30a)
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra"—this is the completion of the sentence. In this way, he speaks of the discourse regarding the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas) among the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtis):
"Dhārikā, Dīpti, Atiyuktā, Jyotsnā, and Caitā—these are exceedingly powerful. (30b)
"Dhātrī, Bahvīśa, and Mūrtīśa are considered [deities] within the scope of the *pīṭhas* and so forth" (32a).

"Śarva and the others"—this is the remainder of the sentence that serves as an exception (*apavāda*). Thus, having set aside the distinction regarding the installation for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), [the text proceeds].

Referring to another type of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), he says: "The Lords [state that] for the practitioner, there is a predominance of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth within the consecration. (32b)
Ananta and the others would indeed be [female], having come under the influence of the threefold recitation (tripāṭha);

that is to say, they would be the powers (śakti) of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara). For it is not the case that femininity is impossible for the Lords of Knowledge. Therefore, the eightfold position is the cause for the fivefold position. Thus ends the [discussion of] the objection.

The primary [powers] are action (kriyā), knowledge (jñāna), and will (icchā); these are the lords of the five forms in the sacred seats (pīṭha) and so forth. Now, the worship of the fierce deities (ugrārcā) is described.

"Ugra" refers to sorcery (*ābhicāra*) and other such minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*) indicated by the word "and. "Arcā" means an image; that is also an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the pedestal and the stone slab therein, he states the eightfold view:
"Delusion, ignorance, the senses, the end, death, fear, and fevers. (33b)
"In the five-fold system, who is the darkness, delusion, trembling, lack of intellect, and lack of shame?
(34a) Having thus explained the distinction between the installation of the *pīṭha*, the stone, and the *mūrtīśas*, [the author] now,
remaining within that very five-fold system, [discusses] those [elements] beginning with earth and ending with space.
Regarding the specific pervasion (*vyāpti*) that pertains to the purpose of constructing the *liṅgas*, *pīṭhas*, and stone slabs for all three types of forms, he says:
"Of all five forms, even in the case of the *liṅgas*, *pīṭhas*, and stone slabs... (34b).
One should contemplate the differentiation [of the levels] according to their pervasion through the principles (*tattva*) in this sequential manner.
(35a) This is self-explanatory. To the question "In what way does that pervasion occur?", he says:
"Up to the end of *rāga* are earth, water, and time; *vidyā* is that, and fire is its end. (35b)

The seat of space (vyomapīṭhaka) extends from Vāyu up to Īśvara and Śiva; the seat of the Liṅga belongs to the Stone (Śilā); the seat of Puruṣa extends to the Earth (Kṣmā), while Water extends up to Māyā as its limit. || 36a-37a ||

The wind [element] ends with Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā); the seat of space (vyomapīṭha) ends with Power (śakti). Earth ends with the elements; water ends with sound; and fire ends with the organs of action.
"Vāyu ends with the intellect and the senses; [the sequence] from space to the intellect ends in stone.

(38a) Now, relying on the eightfold alternative, he states the ritual of meditating upon the pervasion of the eight forms beginning with Earth within the *liṅga*, the pedestal, the slab, and the stone:

In the eight-fold arrangement, however, the forms beginning with Kṣmā and ending with Īśa are located starting from the east and ending in the northeast; this is the completion of the sentence [referring to] the eightfold manner. Relying on another alternative, he says: "In the five-fold arrangement, [they are] in the west, north, and so forth, resting upon Pūrveśvara. (40a)

The phrase "the five forms" refers to those beginning with Earth and ending with Space; this is the completion of the sentence. One should meditate on each [element] presided over by its corresponding deity—Earth by Satya-Brahmā, Water by Vāmadeva, Fire by Aghora, Air by Tatpuruṣa, and Space by Īśāna-Brahmā—and likewise, Agni-Aghora is presided over in the north.
The southern [direction] is presided over by Brahmā, and the wind [direction] is presided over by Tatpuruṣa;
the eastern [direction] is presided over by Vyomeśa, and it should be meditated upon as being presided over by Īśāna and Brahmā in the northeast—this is the intended meaning.
Thus, this is the meditation on the arrangement of the Mūrtis and Mūrtīśas upon the Liṅga, the Pīṭha, and the stones.
The sequence has been stated.

Now, anticipating the question of how it is with regard to images (pratimā), he states the specific detail while extending the aforementioned method to them as well: "This entire sequence should be understood to apply to images too. (40b)

However, the placement of the three principles (*tattva-nyāsa*) extends from the knees to the neck and head; for it has been stated that the *ātmatattva* is placed up to the knees, the *vidyātattva* up to the neck, and the *śivatattva* up to the head, and thus they are established in this sequence. As for the other sequence, it is as follows:
As it was previously stated (p.
49), that [procedure] must be performed; thus, the three realities apply to both the consecration of the gateway and the palace.
Having studied the very arrangement, he states its division:

"One should contemplate the pervasiveness of the three-part [mantra] upon the doors, the *udumbara* posts, and the branches; likewise, one should contemplate it within the temple, from the base (*jaṅghā*) and the neck (*galaka*) up to the pinnacle (*cūḍā*). (41b)
This is the intended meaning: having divided the door into three sections, that which begins from the *udumbara* [post] is the *ātmatattva* pervading the lower section;
the *vidyātattva* pervades the middle section; and by means of the upper *udumbara*, it pervades the upper [section].

One should meditate upon the Śivatattva as pervading the upper section together with it. Likewise, having divided the temple into three parts— up to the base (jaṅghā), up to the neck (gala), and up to the crest (cūḍā)— and having contemplated their pervasion according to the stated sequence, the placement (nyāsa) of the three tattvas should be performed.
Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the installation of Gaurī and others, he establishes the method for the arrangement of knowledge, as in the case of the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*):
"In the installation of Gaurī and others, [one should place] Śakti, whose nature is action, upon the pedestal. (42b)
The wise one should place [the mantras] upon the body; the remainder should be performed as in the case of the pedestal. This is clear.
In the consecration of a face-liṅga, when the pedestal has been divided into nine squares,
one should place the principle of Sadāśiva, namely Īśvara, in the center, and [the principle of Śuddhavidyā] in the east.
One should place the Vidyā in the southeast, Māyā in the south, and then Kālāgni in the southwest; one should place Yatim in the west, Rāga in the northwest, and Nara in the north.
Pradhāna is in the direction of Īśa (the northeast), and the five Brahmans are in their own respective directions. || 45 ||
This is clear. Regarding the specific procedure for the deposition of the three principles (*tattva*), he says:
"The conceptualization of the three principles is as before; however, Sadāśiva is [placed] within the circle" (46a, p.
One should install the half-form as before, as well as the presiding deities of the forms (mūrtīśvaras).
The meaning is clear. Now, having removed the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the entire collection of objects, [one should understand] how the nature of the Śiva-liṅga is for one who knows the Self.

In that very place, for one who is sinking part by part [into dissolution], he contemplates [the elements] as the foundation to be established as the seed, [visualizing them] through their spatial nature;
then, these nine principles and so forth [he contemplates] even within the images of the earth. (47b)

Having meditated upon the pervasion, the seed-syllable, the name, and the form of Mūrti, Mūrtīśvara, and the others, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) everywhere according to their established positions. || 48 ||
The phrase "even in the case of images" (pratimāsvapi) includes, by virtue of the word "even" (api), the lingas and clay figurines as well;

moreover, it applies everywhere to all things to be consecrated, such as temples and so forth, which was previously mentioned. Therefore, this [consecration] is established upon the consideration of both the general and specific causes.
It has been stated that, having performed [the preliminary rites], the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be carried out according to the established procedure.

The nine principles (*tattva*) beginning with Sadāśiva and those beginning with the Earth principle have been declared as being situated upon the pedestal of the face-liṅga once it has been made into nine parts. The armor (*varma*) consisting of the principles beginning with Earth is taught; the forms (*mūrti*) are eightfold and fivefold.

The earth and the other [elements], whose forms are the [deities] beginning with Śarva, are the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) ending with Bhairava in the eightfold system; however, in the fivefold system, they are the Lords of Causes beginning with Brahmā, namely the five Brahmās, and by the word "etcetera," the three qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas) as well as knowledge, action, and will.
It indicates;
it indicates the mutual integration of the words of the *Vyāpti-sūkta* by way of their being possessed of a logical cause (*hetumat*).
In the absence of such integration, there would be an absence of connection with the Supreme, and consequently, an absence of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

Because the use of the word "seed" (*bīja*) implies that independent, collective agency is not established; [this applies] to the connection of those things mentioned as being of the nature of the self (*ātman*).

The cause leads one to understand the command of Īśvara. Furthermore, because nowhere does it transcend the womb of Vāgīśvara, it indicates both the nature of sound and the state of being cognizable by sound; for there is no object whatsoever that is not sound.
Thus he says; by this, it is stated that the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and other rites are to be accomplished through mantras.
Up to the seventh form, he designates the bodies solely by means of the causes to be mentioned later, for there is no [designation] for those who have transcended [the stages].
Having understood that the descent [of the deity] occurs for those characterized by a body,
and that the nature of one who is partless (*niṣkala*) is such that their movement is bound, because of the deficiency in performing the ritual practice,
therefore, having meditated upon all this, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) must be performed; such is the definition of the aphorism.
This is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
Now, he explains what was stated [in verse 48] regarding "when it exists":
"But the earth, remaining in its state as water, [remains] within its own respective domain, such as that of water and so forth. (49a)

It should be understood that the relationship between the ten principles beginning with Earth and ending with the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*)— in terms of their nature as obscuring coverings (*āvaraṇa-bhāva*), their relationship as cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*), and their relationship as support and supported (*āśrayāśrayī-bhāva*)—
has been stated here. In this context, Earth and the others are included within the five forms (*pañca-mūrtayaḥ*).
He states the quarter [of the verse] concerning the abiding of the powers such as *aṇimā* within the form of the *mūrti*:

"The two, Soma and Sūrya, are established in the form of the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*). And above those two is that which is called Dharma; Dharma is established by the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) as consisting of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices. (49b)
He who has that very thing called "sacrifice" as his designation is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), meaning the Peak (*kūṭa*).
Thus, the abiding state of the eight forms (*mūrti*) has been described. Now, he states the locations of the presiding deities of those forms:
Śarva is established in smell;
Ruccas, Paśubhṛt, and likewise Ugra are in the sphere of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).

Rudra, whose nature consists solely of the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra), is to be understood as being right there; Īśāna resides in the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra), while Mahādeva is situated in the mind (manas). || 51 ||
And Bhīma resides in the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra); such is the established order of the Lords of the Mūrtis.

Here, in accordance with the nature of the Lords of the Mūrtis, their installation in the northern direction and so forth is performed according to a graduated scale, and this same principle should be understood to apply to those [deities] who will be mentioned hereafter as well.

Thus, the Lords of Form (mūrtīśas) have been described for one seeking liberation; now he speaks of them for one seeking enjoyment: "The Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) are to be known as established in the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). (52b)
Even the presiding deities of the forms (mūrtipās) are observed in minor rites,
because their nature consists of the concealment of illusion (māyāpidhānamaya), owing to the state of the objects being otherwise established.
Now, relying on the fivefold division, he demonstrates only the five Kalās as the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas).
O Acyuta, [the sequence] from Earth up to Puruṣa has Brahmā as its beginning and extends to Māyā; [the sequence] from Earth up to Vidyā has Rudra as its beginning and extends to Īśvara;
[the sequence] from Earth up to Nāda has Sādākhya as its beginning and extends to Śakti; [and the sequence] from Earth up to Parā has [Śiva] as its limit.

Because they abide within the power that has the earth as its limit (*kṣmavadhiśakti*), it is proclaimed that all the Lords of Form (*mūrtīśa*) consist of power (*śaktimaya*), both directly and through lineage.
For power is indeed the body; moreover, power consists of the enjoyment of form, and the earring (*kuṇḍala*) itself is the embodied form.

Because of its nature as a category. Furthermore, the word "supreme" (para) indicates two states of this Śivaliṅga, which is identical with Śiva. In the state of being non-supreme (apara), the word "supreme" is excluded.

(53) The gurus maintain that because Śiva consists of the supreme state (*parāvasthā*), the extraction of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇoddhāraṇa*) is pervaded by the supreme state within the *liṅga* which is the form of Śiva. Such, then, is the [nature] of the Śiva-liṅga.

The statement that "the entire sphere of resonance (*dhvaniveśabhūmi*) is the *ālaya*" means that it is the nature of the *ālaya*. Now, in order to indicate that even those who possess mastery over that [sphere] do not have a different state of being because they are merely a portion of it, he demonstrates their abiding within the later stages.
The ten incarnate forms of Viṣṇu are established in the principle of Earth (pṛthivī-tattva).
Sustained by my intellect, they are within the range of the Guṇas, the Puruṣas, and the Vidyeśvaras.
Mitrā and the others, Keśava and the others, the three Pākas, and the twelve [forms] are thus of three kinds.
In the principle called Sādākhya, there is the goddess Sarasvatī of Vighnarāja; in Śuddhavidyā, there are Nandin and the others; and in the sphere of Īśvara, there is Lakṣmī.
Established in Prakṛti by a portion [of her own nature], she resides in the intellect through [limited] power;
in the Puruṣa, she is the Pāñcarātra, and Śiva resides in the Sun.
Apsaras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, vidyādharas, and indeed kinnaras; bhūtas, vetālas, ḍākinīs, planets, lunar mansions, and zodiac signs. || 57 ||

The oceans, the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas), and others; the sages (ṛṣis), Brahmā and the other lords of the directions (gīśvaras); as well as those born from a womb, from an egg, and from sprouts—these are to be known as residing in the principle (tattva) of the Earth.
Likewise, wherever else there is a stable abiding among the principles, [they are to be understood in that same way].

What is the basis for the continuity of logic? That very thing is indeed its supreme state. This is the intended meaning: now, what is the proof that this is their supreme state as it has been set forth? And what is the reason for accepting it as such, both in the case of the lamp and in the case of [the mind] being accepted in that manner?
"Starting precisely from that grasper," thus [it is said] regarding the acceptance of their respective scriptures by all the *samayins*.

If it is asked: "Since there is no disagreement among those who proclaim their own respective systems as the supreme state, when doubt regarding the truth arises, whose [position] represents the ultimate reality? we reply: "It belongs only to that which is endowed with reason (*nyāya*).
Reason is the exclusive means for determining the nature of things, free from partiality toward any particular position.

Therefore, having abandoned the boat [of ignorance], what seeker of truth would not, within a year, purify their own self as a witness and accept the ultimate reality? Thus, there is nothing illogical here.

He begins to describe, in sequence, the specific components such as the vajra and other suitable objects like ornaments; these are explained as required, by way of brief, primary, and detailed expositions.

She has four faces and eight arms, wears yellow and non-yellow garments, possesses a gentle form upon the tortoise, and is surrounded by the serpent-ocean and rivers. (62) Mounted upon a ram, with blazing rays—thus are the guardians of the forms beginning with Śarva described. (79a)
Up to this point, it is clear. This is according to the eightfold system (*aṣṭapakṣa*). Now, regarding the fivefold system (*pañcapakṣa*), he says:
"Having the appearance of molten gold, adorned with four arms and the moon, holding a vajra, an abhaya-gesture, and a rosary—this is proclaimed as Nivṛtti," and so forth.

"Endowed with a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a rosary, she bestows the boons of *śāntyatītā*. This much is clear. (84a) These are the five forms. Now, he describes the five guardians of these forms (*mūrtipas*):
"Wearing the attire of a youth (*bāla*), three-eyed, with a full crescent moon as his crest-ornament. (84b)
"Immediately [he becomes] one without earrings, with eyes like lotuses," and so forth, up to:
"In his left hands, he holds a khaṭvāṅga, a spear, a trident, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (85a, p. 55)
This is clear. Furthermore, he states eight alternative views, beginning with:

"The Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) have four faces and ten arms like Hara," and so forth, ending with: "The Vidyeśvara is said to be endowed with weapons and surrounded by the single quality of Īśāna. This is clear.
Furthermore, he speaks of five [forms] in the section:
"Brahmā has four faces, is yellow, and is adorned with four staff-like arms," and so forth;
"Sadāśiva has ten arms, a serene face, and five faces. (93b)
Up to this point, the meaning is clear. Regarding the three principles (*tattva*), he says:
"Four-armed, four-faced, seated upon a square lotus" (94a), and so forth, ending with:
"This is indeed remembered as the Śiva-principle, five-faced and four-armed."
This is clear. Thus, the forms of the deities presiding over the forms, which constitute their objects of meditation, have been described.
Now, he states the fault that arises from performing these [rites] at places or times other than those prescribed:
Sacrifices performed only in one's own country and at the proper time bestow the desired fruit.
One should worship the region and the time, beginning with the southeast direction (Āgneyī).
Having invoked one's own eight chosen deities and having established the region outside [the altar], [one should proceed].
From one's own twelve-fold time-cycle, from one's own ritual action, and from one's own year. || 99 ||
The five regions have been obtained from the earth, and the eight [groups] starting with Amareśa follow in sequence.
Even in another region or at another time, those very same [factors] are the causes of misfortune;
therefore, one should perform the preparation of the place and time during the consecration ceremony.
And Time, beginning with its manifestation, proceeds according to a twelvefold sequence.

And others, situated within those [lines] that pervade it, as well as the regions and the channels (*nāḍikā*).
Having divided the temple-site (*prāsādakṣetra*) into eight parts, there should be nine lines facing east and as many facing north; thus, there are eighteen lines.
Regarding the term "named *nāḍī*":
both bamboo poles placed at the corners [of the square] have eight ropes as their six feet.

Then, by means of a cord (rajju) joined to this region and so forth, wherever a step (pada) is to be placed, there and then at that very time, one should place it; thus indeed.

"The Mūrtīśas grant the fruits of one's desired objects. Thus [ends the section]. Now, in connection with the regions (deśa), the presiding deities of the objects are shown. To the question "How many are there, and what are their names?", he says:
"Brahmeśa, Parjanya, Jaya, Mahendra, Ravi, Satyaka," [and so forth].

From "iti" up to "tripañcāśatpadam" (fifty-three squares), the meaning is clear. Now, having stated "athopadam" (and then the squares), the explanation begins with "atho" regarding the form of the *vāstu*.
He begins to speak:

"The lines for the eastern and northern [directions] consist of eight finger-breadths. Eight lines of the bamboo frame, when joined together, form both [sides]. They should be made with their ends facing the corners; such is the method."
The distinction is as follows: each of the four cords should consist of three mantra-padas, while the interior of the fourfold [grid] consists of six pada-s each;
thus, in the sixty-four-pada Vāstu, it should be arranged accordingly. This is easily understood.
Now, he begins to describe, according to their respective locations on the site-plan, the fifty-three deities previously mentioned, as well as those numbering five:
Having designated the deities here according to the sequence of three, three, and five [units], Brahmā is in the center on four units; immediately after that, Marīci is on six units.
After Brahmā, in the next row, there are two units; outside of that row, having bowed, it is thus "Nati" and so forth.

There is a six-footed [verse] regarding the rays (*marīci*). With reference to two additional squares in the southeast corner (*āgneya-koṇa*) of those very same rows, he says, "Of Savitṛ, in the southeast corner," and so forth, ending with "Rudradāsa, let him go even further than that. This is clear. He recites [the verse] for the northerners at Śivayakṣa.
Regarding "śa" and so forth, he says in the northeast:
"āva-stv-īśānyata" and so on. Now, concerning the single row [of syllables] all around the exterior, he speaks starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise.

"Starting from the half-square of Īśāna," and so forth: in the location of the square of Īśāna in the northeast corner, there is Īśāna; then, starting from the southern square, [there are] Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendra, Ravi, Satyaka, and Bhrāśā—this group of six [occupies] the half of the square of the southeast corner (Āgneya).

In the middle of the space between the directions is Saptārcis (the seven-rayed one). Following that, starting from the southwest (paścimādārabhya), there is a group of six squares for Pūṣan, Vitatha, Graha, Kṣata, Pretapati, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅga. In the half-square of the Nirṛti corner is Mṛga, and in the other half is Pitṛ.
Then, beginning from the northern cell, there are six lords: Pitṛda, Vāra, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Pracetas, and Asura Śeṣa.
Furthermore, in half of the wind-cell, [there is] Aditi-roga; thus [there are] thirty-two.
In the half of the hundred-square [grid], there is *Romaśadya*; in its half, starting from the eastern square, are Vāyu, Nāgamukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, and others occupying six squares each;
furthermore, in the half of the northeast square of the *Kroṣṭu*, there is *Īti*—thus, there are thirty-two deities.
Having visualized [the deities] in a clockwise sequence, they are to be worshipped. Thus, beginning with Brahmā in the center, he concludes the number of those Vāstu-deities to be worshipped (p.
Thus, forty-five deities reside within the body of the *vāstu*.
Now, regarding the worship of the Rākṣasīs on the exterior of the *vāstu* body, at the end of the four corner squares starting from Īśāna, he says:
"Carakī and Vidārī," and so forth; these four [deities] are likewise outside, in sequence, ending with verse 115.
Having thus described the sixty-four-padded site-plan (*vāstu*), he now describes the eighty-one-padded planetary site-plan (*grahavāstu*).
"In the eighty-one-square Vāstu, [the central portion] extends up to nine squares," and so forth.

(118b) He concludes the section on the measurement of time regarding the nature of the sequence of lines he himself has commenced.

Having collected [the teachings] at the proper time with the desire for their completion,
the venerable teacher Soma-Bhṛṅgu compiled two hundred works from the various Āgamas.
At the proper time, [one should quickly place] one or the other of those two respective seed-syllables called Śrī and Varuṇa.
